0.title: Blueprint
0.content: The blueprint is the automation each room runs. This page covers every input and how a room behaves. Its settings come in two groups. Customise holds what most rooms change: a section for each phase, and Custom for anything more particular. Fine Tuning holds what most rooms never touch. This page follows the same order. On this page . | Room | Phases . | Idle brightness | Scenes | . | Custom . | Brightness template | Additional triggers | . | Sensors & Conditions . | Wait time | Lux Threshold | Conditions | Trigger IDs | . | Transitions | Other Settings . | Override protection | Prefer RGB during | Stored traces | Sensors from areas | Additional trigger entities | . | How a room behaves . | When the room updates | When lights turn on and off | Why didn’t my light change? | . | Turning override protection off | Updating the blueprint | .

1.title: Room
1.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Schedule | required | The FLARE schedule the room follows. | . | Lights & Occupancy | required | The room’s lights, and the occupancy and motion sensors that turn them on and off. An illuminance sensor picked here, or in its area, drives Lux Threshold. | . Lights & Occupancy takes an area, a floor, a device, a label, or individual entities. When you target an area, floor, device, or label, lights and sensors added to it later are included automatically. FLARE picks the room’s lights the same way Home Assistant does when you call light.turn_on on that target: . | A light you pick by name is always included. | A hidden light is left out if it was picked through an area, floor, device or label. | A configuration or diagnostic light, such as the indicator light on a wall switch, is left out if it was picked through an area, floor or device, or a label on its device or area. If the label is on the light itself, it’s included. | . The room’s flare controls the same lights. Sensors are binary_sensor entities with device_class: occupancy or device_class: motion; other binary sensors in the target are ignored. A room can mix both kinds. To pick an area for its lights but leave some of its sensors out, add them with Exclude target. A room with no sensor follows the schedule but never turns its lights on or off. A physical room can have more than one FLARE automation — for example, one for a lamp and another for the ceiling light. Each automation releases the lights it drives once all of them are off, so if the same light appears in both automations, its override is cleared when either automation’s lights go dark.

2.title: Phases
2.content: Morning, Day, Evening and Night each have a section with the same three settings, which apply while the schedule is in that phase. | Input | Default | Description | . | Lights Off | none | Lights in the room that stay off during the phase. | . | Idle Brightness | 0 | The brightness, 0–255, the room’s lights dim to when it’s empty, instead of switching off. 0 turns them off. | . | Scene | none | A scene the room uses instead of the schedule during the phase. | . Idle brightness . An idle brightness turns a room’s “off” state into a dim glow, acting as a nightlight. It only works in a room with occupancy or motion sensors, since a sensorless room never becomes empty. Outside of running the automation manually, idle brightness is the only way lights come on while the room is empty. For a nightlight whenever it’s dark outside, leave each phase at 0 and set the Idle Brightness Template to: . {{ 10 if is_state('sun.sun', 'below_horizon') else {} }} . See Templates for one lamp as the nightlight, and other variations. Scenes . A scene is only used if every entity it sets is in the room; otherwise the whole room follows the schedule. When a scene is used, any light in the room that the scene doesn’t set still follows the schedule. See Scene handoff.

3.title: Custom
3.content: Templates for when per-phase settings aren’t enough, like dimming the room while the TV is on. Whenever a template returns a value, it overrides the per-phase setting. | Input | Default | Description | . | Brightness Template | none | A template returning a mapping of entity ID to brightness, in place of the schedule’s. When it returns a light, its value overrides Lights Off for that light. | . | Idle Brightness Template | none | Like Brightness Template, for when the room is empty (except 'x0.5'). When it returns a light, its value overrides Idle Brightness for that light; 0, '0%', null, or false turns the light off when empty. | . | Scene Template | none | A template returning a scene’s entity ID, or '' for none. When it returns a scene that exists, it overrides the phase’s Scene. | . | Additional Triggers | none | Triggers that make the room update as soon as they fire. | . Brightness template . | Value | Effect | . | 1–255 | Sets the light to this brightness, on the same scale as the phase brightnesses. | . | '50%' | Sets the light to this percentage of full brightness: '100%' is 255, '50%' is 128, as for light.turn_on’s brightness_pct. | . | 'x0.5' | Sets the light to the schedule’s brightness multiplied by this, so 'x0.5' is half of it. | . | 0, '0%' or 'x0' | Turns the light off. | . | null or false | FLARE leaves the light alone, including when the room empties, and its being on doesn’t count as the room being in use. | . A single value instead of a mapping applies to every light in the room, and any light the template doesn’t include follows the schedule. Idle Brightness Template accepts the same values except 'x0.5', and returning 0, '0%', null, or false turns the light off when the room empties (unlike Brightness Template, null here does not leave the light alone). The templates can read brightness: the schedule’s brightness right now (0–255), or none while the schedule is unavailable. See Templates. Additional triggers . Add a trigger for anything a template depends on, such as a State trigger on the TV for a Brightness Template that dims the room while it’s playing. These are the same triggers as an ordinary automation’s, so each trigger can be as specific as you need: the TV changing to playing, an attribute, a button press, or a time. An additional trigger only adjusts lights that are already on, and never switches lights on in an empty dark room. To turn a room on from something else, see lighting a room from a remote.

4.title: Sensors & Conditions
4.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Wait Time | 120s | How long every occupancy and motion sensor must be clear before the room is empty. | . | Lux Threshold | 0 (off) | Above 0, the room stays dark while every illuminance sensor in it reads above this many lux. | . | Conditions | none | As in an ordinary automation: all must be met for the room to run. While they aren’t, the room is paused. | . Wait time . Most occupancy and motion sensors clear the moment they stop seeing movement, even with someone sitting still. The room counts as empty only once every one of them has been clear for the Wait Time. It isn’t used in a room without sensors. Lux Threshold . Illuminance sensors are the sensor entities with device_class: illuminance in Lights & Occupancy — picked by name, or included through its area, floor, device or label — that aren’t excluded. When Sensors From Areas is off, only the sensors picked by name count. When Lux Threshold is above 0, the room counts as bright enough while every working illuminance sensor in it reads above the threshold. While the room is bright enough, FLARE leaves off lights off even when: . | an occupancy or motion sensor detects someone, | a scene applies (unless every light the scene covers is already on), or | idle brightness would otherwise dim the room. | . If someone is still in the room when the light level drops to the threshold or below, the lights come on right away. Someone counts as in the room if one of its occupancy or motion sensors is detecting them, or stopped detecting them within the Wait Time. Lights that are already on continue following the curve or stay in the phase’s scene; FLARE never switches lights off just because a room is bright. Turning the room on by hand — via the automation’s Run actions, its flare, or a voice assistant controlling the flare — ignores Lux Threshold. An illuminance sensor that is unavailable, unknown, or non-numeric is ignored, and a room with no working illuminance sensors never skips turning on. The threshold check is disabled while Lux Threshold is 0, which is the default. Conditions . While any of the Conditions isn’t met, the room does nothing at all: its lights stay as they are, sensors don’t turn it on or off, and the schedule isn’t followed. For a vacation or guest mode, add a State condition on an input_boolean. Once every condition is met again, the room catches up on its next regular update: lights that are on move to the schedule, and an empty room turns off. If a condition reads an entity, add a trigger for it to Additional Triggers so the room catches up as soon as it changes. Running the automation by hand, or turning on its flare, still works while the room is paused. A room that was already lit when the pause starts stays on until the pause ends (or you switch it off yourself). To block only specific triggers — for example, so a pet walking through at night doesn’t switch the lights on, while turning off and following the schedule still run — add a Triggered by condition checking one of the trigger IDs: . condition: not conditions: - condition: and conditions: - condition: trigger id: - motion_on - lux_dark - condition: time after: "23:00:00" before: "06:00:00" . Trigger IDs . Each of the room’s triggers has an ID, which a Triggered by condition in Conditions can check. Home Assistant’s editor can’t list a blueprint’s triggers, so the condition shows a warning and no choices: use ⋮ → Edit in YAML and type the ID, as in the example above. | ID | Fires when | . | phase_change | the schedule moves to another phase | . | tick | the room’s regular update, about once a minute | . | motion_on | an occupancy or motion sensor detects someone | . | motion_off | a sensor has been clear for the Wait Time | . | lux_dark | the room stops being too bright for Lux Threshold, with someone there | . | recovered | one of the room’s lights comes back online | . | extra | an entity in Additional Trigger Entities changes (deprecated) | . | your own | one of your Additional Triggers fires: the ID you give it, or its position if it has none | . Give each of your Additional Triggers an ID if a condition needs to tell them apart. Whatever ID you give a custom trigger, it still behaves as an additional trigger — naming a trigger motion_on won’t make it switch the lights on. Running the automation by hand has no trigger, and skips Conditions anyway.

5.title: Transitions
5.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Turning On | 1s | How long lights take to fade up when someone comes in, or when you run the automation by hand. | . | Turning Off | 15s | How long lights take to fade out once the room is empty. | . | Everything Else | 5s | How long every other update takes, such as the schedule moving on. | .

6.title: Other Settings
6.content: | Input | Default | Description | . | Override Protection | on | Leaves a light alone once something else changes it, until all of the room’s lights are off. | . | Prefer RGB During | Evening, Night | Phases in which lights that support RGB are sent an RGB colour instead of a colour temperature. | . | Stored Traces | 20 | How many of the automation’s recent runs keep a trace. | . | Sensors From Areas | on | When off, sensors aren’t inferred from the areas, floors, devices or labels in Lights & Occupancy; only explicitly selected sensors are used. Deprecated: use Exclude target instead of turning this off. | . | Additional Trigger Entities | none | Entities that make the room update as soon as they change. Deprecated: use Additional Triggers instead. | . Override protection . Turn it off for a room whose bulbs misreport. Prefer RGB during . Many bulbs give richer warm colours in RGB, but their cool whites can look blue, so the default leaves Morning and Day on colour temperature. Stored traces . A room updates every minute, so the default keeps about the last 20 minutes of runs in the automation’s Traces. Raise it while you’re tracking down something that happened earlier; each trace takes memory, so set it back once you’re done. Sensors from areas . If you turn Sensors From Areas off, only the sensors you pick by name in Lights & Occupancy count, so you can select an area for its lights while picking sensors from elsewhere (such as the hallway’s sensors for a landing). If you pick no sensors at all, the room only follows the schedule without turning its lights on or off automatically. Sensors From Areas is deprecated, and FLARE 3.0 removes it. It only shows in a room that has it turned off. Use Exclude target in Lights & Occupancy instead of turning it off, to leave out the sensors you don’t want (see Home Assistant’s excluding targets). An excluded sensor doesn’t count, whether it came from an area, a device, a floor or a label. Additional trigger entities . A list of entities that trigger a room update whenever any of them changes state, equivalent to adding State triggers for those entities in Additional Triggers. Additional Trigger Entities is deprecated, and FLARE 3.0 removes it. Move each entity to Additional Triggers as a State trigger, then clear this list.

7.title: How a room behaves
7.content: When the room updates . A room updates straight away when the phase changes, a sensor detects someone, or an Additional Trigger fires, and 5 seconds after its lights come back online when the whole room was unavailable. Between those events, it updates on the tick of the first area in Lights & Occupancy, which is every minute by default. A room whose Lights & Occupancy names no area updates every minute, on the minute. When lights turn on and off . Lights turn on when a sensor detects someone, and turn off once every sensor in the room has been clear for the Wait Time. While every light FLARE controls in Lights & Occupancy is off, the only things that turn any of them on are a sensor detecting someone, running the automation by hand, the room dropping below Lux Threshold while someone is in it, and idle brightness. Once at least one light is on, any update can turn on the others. That way, a phase change never lights up an empty room, and a bulb that comes back online stays off if the rest of the room is off. On each regular update or phase change while the room has been empty for the Wait Time, if any light that shouldn’t be idle is still on, FLARE sends the turn-off command again. Running the automation by hand sets every light in the room, including ones someone else has changed. Why didn’t my light change? . | Someone else changed it. If a light was changed from a wall switch, an app, a voice assistant, or another automation (including being switched off), FLARE leaves it alone until every light in the room is off. See override protection. | The room’s Conditions aren’t met, so it’s paused. The automation’s Traces show the Conditions step that stopped it. | The room is empty and the light was off. See when lights turn on and off. | The room is above Lux Threshold, so off lights stay off even when motion is detected. | It’s already close enough. Changes smaller than 5% of the brightness or 5 mireds of colour temperature aren’t sent. You can change both tolerances under FLARE → Settings → Configure. | It’s unavailable. FLARE sets it once it comes back online. | An active scene covers it, or Brightness Template returns null for it. | It’s at its idle brightness. See idle brightness. | It isn’t one of the room’s lights. A hidden light, or a configuration or diagnostic light, isn’t included through an area, floor, device or label. Pick it directly in Lights & Occupancy to include it. See Room. | .

8.title: Turning override protection off
8.content: Override protection works by reading back what each light reports, and checking it against what FLARE last sent. Bulbs don’t always report what they’re actually showing: some send an old value for a moment after reconnecting, some report colour in a different mode from the one they were sent, and some settle outside the colour range they advertise. When a bulb reports values that don’t match what FLARE sent, it becomes overridden even though nobody touched it, and FLARE leaves it alone until every light in the room is off. If a room’s lights keep getting stuck like this, first try raising the tolerances under FLARE → Settings → Configure (see how close counts as a match). If that doesn’t help, you can turn off Override Protection in the room’s automation. FLARE then stops tracking overrides for that room and sets any light that isn’t already close enough to the curve on every update, which means: . | A light someone else changes, from a wall switch, an app or another automation, goes back to the curve at the next update. | A light switched off by hand comes back on at the next update while the room is occupied. | If you set the room’s flare to a brightness or colour, for example by asking a voice assistant for 100%, the room goes back to the curve at the next update. Turning the flare on and off works as usual. | . A room with override protection off isn’t counted in the Overrides view. If you turn override protection off because of your bulbs, please open an issue with their make and model, so FLARE can learn to read them properly.

9.title: Updating the blueprint
9.content: The blueprint comes with FLARE, so after each FLARE update a repair appears under Settings → System → Repairs offering the new copy. Press Fix to install it; your automations keep their settings. If you’ve edited the blueprint file yourself, ignore the repair, because installing replaces your changes. FLARE installs the blueprint in Home Assistant’s language (Settings → System → General) when it has a translation for it (currently German), and in English otherwise. If you change Home Assistant’s language, the same repair offers the blueprint in the new language. Its Details links lead to this page, in English.

10.title: Claims and override protection
10.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. Override protection is FLARE leaving a light alone once someone else has changed it. It hangs on one question, asked fresh on every write: is this light still showing what FLARE last did to it? The answer comes from comparing the light’s live state with a record of FLARE’s own writes, its claims. There’s no “overridden” flag set once by a trigger. A trigger firing once blocks only the run it fires in (lesson 2 in CLAUDE.md). Re-asking against live state every time is what makes everything else fall out: room-empty, light-off and reconnect releases all just happen.

11.title: The pieces
11.content: | Module | Holds | Pure? | . | tracking/override_protection.py | classify(), the decision table, and classify_state(), its adapter for a live HA state | yes | . | tracking/matching.py | shows(): does a light’s report match a target? | yes | . | tracking/claims.py | ClaimRegistry: claims, rooms, the Store, the state listener | no | . | sensor.py | ClaimEvents (statuses, events), the counts, each light’s status sensor | no | .

12.title: The data
12.content: classDiagram class ClaimRegistry { claims: dict~entity_id, WriteRecord~ rooms: dict~room_key, Room~ status(entity_id) async_record(room, lights, context, targets) async_override(room, lights) async_clear(lights) } class WriteRecord { observed: ContextClaim | None latest: ContextClaim | None mismatch_since: iso | absent } class ContextClaim { context_id secondary_context_id recorded_at target: dict | None } class Room { lights: list~entity_id~ } ClaimRegistry "1" --> "*" WriteRecord ClaimRegistry "1" --> "*" Room WriteRecord --> ContextClaim : observed WriteRecord --> ContextClaim : latest . One claim per light, whichever caller wrote it, so two automations driving the same light never mistake each other’s writes for overrides. Two claims in each record: . | latest is FLARE’s most recent write, not yet seen landing. | observed is a state FLARE can safely write over: a write it has seen land, or for a light’s first-ever write, the context it had just before and what it was showing then. | . On each new write, if the light’s live context matches latest, that write landed and is promoted to observed. If it still matches observed, the write never landed and observed stays as it was. Either way the light is still FLARE’s, so a dropped write can’t lock FLARE out, even if the light reports the same state again under a new context. A target is what a write asked for — {brightness, color_temp_kelvin}, {brightness, rgb_color}, or {"state": "off"} for a turn-off — stored in the exact form Home Assistant sends to the light (matching.sent()). For example, if a light can’t take Kelvin directly, a Kelvin target is stored as the RGB values Home Assistant converts and sends instead. If a light reports back under an unrelated context (for instance, after Home Assistant drops the call’s context 5 seconds later), it still counts as FLARE’s as long as its state matches the target. A room identifies the caller (room_id, which for the blueprint is the automation entity), keyed by its entity registry ID so renaming the automation preserves its room. A room’s light list includes its latest room_entities, every light it has written to, and any light it still holds a claim on, so all of those claims can be released together when the room goes dark. A call with no room_id writes to the lights without reading or recording claims — that is what the blueprint’s Override Protection toggle controls.

13.title: Deciding: classify()
13.content: flowchart TB S(["light state + record"]) --> R{"reachable?"} R -->|"no"| UN["unavailable"] R -->|"yes"| NC{"any claim?"} NC -->|"no"| ONQ{"on?"} ONQ -->|"yes"| UT1["untracked"] ONQ -->|"no"| OFF["off"] NC -->|"yes"| CTX{"live context =<br/>latest or observed?"} CTX -->|"yes"| CON1["controlled"] CTX -->|"no"| ISON{"on?"} ISON -->|"no"| ASKOFF{"a claim asked for off?"} ASKOFF -->|"yes"| CON2["controlled"] ASKOFF -->|"no, no observed"| UT2["untracked"] ASKOFF -->|"no"| OV1["disagrees"] ISON -->|"yes"| OBS{"observed exists?"} OBS -->|"no"| UT3["untracked"] OBS -->|"yes"| VAL{"shows latest's or<br/>observed's target?"} VAL -->|"yes"| CON3["controlled"] VAL -->|"no"| OV2["disagrees"] OV1 --> GR{"mismatch_since older<br/>than 30 s?"} OV2 --> GR GR -->|"yes"| OVR["overridden"] GR -->|"no"| MM["mismatched"] . overridden and mismatched both block: grouping leaves the light out unless the call has force. The difference is only in what’s reported. A light becomes overridden once its mismatch has lasted 30 seconds (MISMATCH_GRACE). Until then it’s mismatched: blocked, so a real change is never written over, but not counted or announced. Most short mismatches are FLARE’s own write still landing, or a bulb reporting a stale value as it reconnects. Being switched off is an override. classify() doesn’t short-circuit on off. FLARE’s own turn-offs record {state: off} as their target, which is how a room switched off at bedtime can come on again but a lamp switched off by hand stays off. Everything that judges a light goes through classify_state(). Grouping calls it through EntityLookup.externally_set(), and the sensors and claims_check through ClaimRegistry.status(). They drifted apart twice when each did its own, and test_one_classifier_adapter.py fails if anything else calls classify(). What a light “shows” (matching.py) . | Check | Rule | . | Brightness | brightness within the Settings tolerance (5% by default), with a minimum floor of 2 points for dim targets. | . | Kelvin | color_temp_kelvin; if reported in xy_color, converted to Kelvin as long as it lies within 0.02 Duv of the Planckian locus. Never read via rgb_color. | . | Same mired | Two Kelvin values that floor to the same mired are treated as equal, because Zigbee bulbs operate in mireds. | . | Near mired | Within the Settings tolerance (5 mireds by default, roughly one just-noticeable difference). | . | Out-of-range target | Matches either the target as asked or the target clamped to the bulb’s advertised min/max range. | . | RGB | rgb_color compared only against an RGB target, by summing channel differences up to twice the colour tolerance (10 by default, minimum floor 4). | . | Kelvin on an RGB-only light | For a light that supports colour but neither color_temp nor rgbww (such as an RGB strip), a Kelvin target is converted via color_temperature_to_hs and compared against rgb_color using the RGB rule. | . | Capability filtering | Brightness isn’t compared on on/off lights, and colour isn’t compared on dimmers, because light.turn_on drops unsupported attributes. A light with unknown supported_color_modes is compared on all attributes. | . matching.py never derives Kelvin from rgb_color: Home Assistant’s Kelvin-to-RGB and xy-to-RGB conversions differ by around 13 in red at 6500 K, so a bulb showing exactly what was asked would fail the check. The only exception is a light that cannot accept Kelvin natively, where Home Assistant itself performs the conversion (color_temperature_to_hs) and the light’s xy report reads 2700 K back as ~1870 K — for those lights, the claim stores and compares the converted RGB target that Home Assistant sends.

15.title: The listener
15.content: ClaimRegistry.async_start_listening follows exactly the claimed lights, through async_track_state_change_event, and re-subscribes whenever the set of claimed lights changes. It follows their registry entries too, with async_track_entity_registry_updated_event. For each change to one: . | Change | Effect | . | any change | note_mismatch: set mismatch_since when it first disagrees, clear it when it matches again | . | on/off → unavailable/unknown (dropped) | its claim is deleted, so its reconnect isn’t read as an override; its rooms are checked for release | . | on/off → off (went off) | each room containing it is released if none of its claimed lights is on | . | none/unavailable/unknown → on/off (arrived) | each room is released if every claimed light has now reported and none is on | . | renamed in the registry | its claim and its place in its rooms move to the new entity ID | . | deleted from the registry | its claim and its place in its rooms are removed | . ClaimRegistry.async_start_listening also follows the registry entry of each entity a room is keyed by. When that automation or entity is deleted, its room is removed along with any claims on lights that no other room tracks (_forget_deleted_rooms, which also runs when claims load at startup). The rules the listener keeps: . | Any state reported while HA is stopping is ignored. MQTT marks lights unavailable as it disconnects, which would drop every claim just before the Store’s final save. | went_off needs a real starting state. Lights reconnect one at a time after a restart, and the first back being off while its siblings are still unknown mustn’t release the room. | Unavailable counts as dark for release, so one dead bulb can’t hold a room open forever. Only claimed lights count, so a TV backlight the room doesn’t drive cannot hold it open either. | .

16.title: Releasing a room
16.content: Once none of a room’s claimed lights is on, the room releases all of its claims (_release_if_dark). Deleting them is deliberate: if a light is later switched on by hand or comes back online from unavailable, it has no claim (untracked), so FLARE takes control of it and sets it to the curve. (Keeping your own brightness or colour from a dark room is what a flare is for.) If a light belongs to two rooms, its claim is released as soon as either room goes dark. Lights that went off while Home Assistant was shut down never fire an on → off state transition on startup, so claims restored from storage run a settled check (release_settled_dark_rooms): a restored room is released once every claimed light in it has reported on or off and none of them is on.

17.title: Persistence
17.content: flowchart LR ch["any claim change"] --> ds["Store.async_delay_save(5 s)"] ds --> file[".storage/flare.claims<br/>{claims, rooms, overrides}"] stop["EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_FINAL_WRITE"] --> file file --> load["next start:<br/>async_load before platforms"] load --> seed["ClaimEvents.start():<br/>seed statuses, note mismatches"] seed --> rel["release rooms restored dark"] . | A restart gives every light a fresh context, so a restored claim can only match by value. A light still showing FLARE’s target stays controlled; one changed before the restart keeps its stored mismatch_since, so it’s overridden at once. | A light deleted while HA was down never sends a registry event. Its restored claim counts as dark, and goes when its room next does. | A crash loses the last 5 seconds of claims and fails open: an unclaimed light is free to drive. | overrides is the override log (log_override), holding the last 50 overrides. Each entry records both claims, the live values, the light’s raw colour attributes (matching.reported()), its device manufacturer and model, the integration providing it, and the active tolerances. Entries are logged when ClaimEvents fires flare_light_overridden (which carries a subset of the same fields) and are surfaced only in the Settings entry’s diagnostics download. | .

18.title: Showing it
18.content: Where claims are stored (the registry and its Store) is separate from how they are presented, and none of the entities hold state of their own: . | Status sensors (sensor.<light>_flare_status) sit on each light’s own device and report what classify_state returns, along with claimed, asked (FLARE’s last target, unrecorded), and rooms. Each sensor updates on its light’s state changes and on SIGNAL_CLAIMS_UPDATED. | Count sensors (sensor.flare_controlled_lights and sensor.flare_overridden_lights) sit on FLARE’s own service device. untracked lights are counted as controlled, since either way they aren’t excluded from updates. | Claim events, fired by ClaimEvents: | . | Event | When | Filed under | . | flare_lights_controlled | a room takes lights it wasn’t driving, gathered for 3 s, lit lights only | the Controlled count | . | flare_light_overridden | a light becomes overridden, with both claims and its live values | the Overridden count | . | flare_lights_released | a room goes dark, or Clear | button.flare_clear | . Each event carries one of FLARE’s entities as entity_id and FLARE’s device_id, which routes it into FLARE’s Activity and lets the dashboard distinguish the three event kinds. A light returning from overridden to controlled is routine state churn rather than news, so no event is fired. The initial refresh after startup seeds statuses silently so restarts don’t flood the logbook.

19.title: Dashboard
19.content: FLARE comes with a ready-made dashboard: a view for each schedule, and one for your rooms. It builds itself from your schedules and rooms each time it loads, so any schedule or room you add later appears on its own. Add it from Settings → Dashboards → Add dashboard: pick FLARE Lighting, then give it a name and an icon. FLARE’s logo is in the icon picker as flare:logo. | A schedule’s view shows the day’s curve and every schedule and curve setting. | Overrides shows how many lights FLARE is controlling, which lights have been taken over, and the last 24 hours of room activity. | .

20.title: In your own dashboard
20.content: The same views can go in a dashboard of your own. Open it, then Edit dashboard → the three-dot menu → Raw configuration editor, and add: . views: - title: Lighting strategy: type: custom:flare-schedule - title: Overrides strategy: type: custom:flare-lights . Like the ready-made dashboard, both views find their own entities each time they load. custom:flare-schedule shows every schedule, one after another. To give each schedule its own view instead, add sensor:: . views: - title: Downstairs strategy: type: custom:flare-schedule sensor: downstairs - title: Upstairs strategy: type: custom:flare-schedule sensor: upstairs . sensor is the part before _flare in the schedule sensor’s entity ID (such as downstairs for sensor.downstairs_flare), or the full entity ID if you’ve renamed the sensor. If sensor doesn’t match any schedule, the view tells you so and lists the schedules you do have.

21.title: Just the chart
21.content: To put the curve chart on a dashboard of your own, add a card, open the By entity tab, and pick your schedule sensor — FLARE Curve appears under Community with a preview. Or add a Manual card in YAML: . type: custom:flare-curve-card sensor: home . sensor is the part before _flare in the schedule sensor’s entity ID, or the full entity ID if you’ve renamed the sensor.

22.title: Reading a schedule’s view
22.content: With over twenty controls on a schedule’s view, two things are colour-coded so you can scan them at a glance: . | Colour is the phase — Morning blue, Day amber, Evening deep orange, Night indigo, wherever that phase appears. | Icon is the channel — brightness, colour temperature, or an hourglass for transitions. | . Each Curve row pairs a colour temperature slider with a brightness slider in that order, so together they preview what the light will look like: both sliders are painted in the colour that phase sets, and how far the brightness slider fills shows how bright the light will be. Copy or paste, at the bottom of each schedule, copies that schedule as text or applies one you paste in, so a schedule can be backed up, shared, or copied onto another schedule. See copying a schedule.

23.title: Reading the Overrides view
23.content: . | All lights at the top shows how many lights FLARE is controlling across the house, how many something else has taken over, and a Clear all button to hand every light back to FLARE at once. | Area cards, grouped by floor, list each room automation’s lights with overridden lights first. The card header shows the area’s controlled and overridden counts along with Clear all for that area, and clicking the area’s name opens its Home Assistant area page. | Each light row shows its status, what FLARE last asked it for, and what it is currently showing (with differing values highlighted in red), plus its own Clear button. Values in amber with an info icon beside them mean the light isn’t showing FLARE’s last change yet, but isn’t overridden either: on a controlled light the command is still taking effect and FLARE keeps retrying it, while on a mismatched light it will become overridden if it doesn’t match again within 30 seconds. Hover over or tap the info icon to see what FLARE asked for, what it last saw the light confirm, and what the light is showing. Click the light’s name to open its more-info dialog. Lights FLARE isn’t currently driving stay hidden behind a Show N untracked row at the bottom of the list. | Activity (beside the areas, or on a separate tab on narrow screens) shows the last 24 hours of room events. Entries are colour-coded — blue when a room starts controlling its lights, amber when something else overrides a light, and grey when a room lets them go — and the filter buttons at the top show one kind at a time. | .

24.title: Changing it
24.content: If you’d rather own the layout and edit it by hand, use Take control from the dashboard’s three-dot menu. Take control is one-way. Once you’ve taken control, the dashboard no longer rebuilds itself, so it won’t pick up changes to FLARE’s layout, and schedules or rooms you add later won’t appear on their own.

25.title: The event loop
25.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. Home Assistant runs one asyncio event loop, and nearly everything FLARE does happens on it, as a reaction to something: a state change, a timer, a service call, a registry update. This page lists every hook and explains the rules they follow.

26.title: Callbacks and coroutines
26.content: Home Assistant code comes in three shapes, and getting the shape wrong fails silently until a real event loop runs it. | Shape | Marked | Runs | FLARE uses it for | . | callback | @callback def | on the loop, to completion, no awaiting | listeners, timers, the claim registry’s writers | . | coroutine | async def | on the loop, yielding at each await | service handlers, setup, anything that calls a service | . | plain function | neither | in the executor (a worker thread) | only file and hashing work, through async_add_executor_job | . A listener or timer handed a plain function that touches hass runs it in a worker thread, where hass.async_create_task raises. That’s lesson 7 in CLAUDE.md, and it’s why every listener here carries @callback. Check core.py’s get_hassjob_callable_job_type before trusting a fix in this area: unit tests don’t catch it. Atomic by construction. A callback can’t be interrupted, so anything done inside one is one step as far as the rest of HA is concerned. The claim registry’s writers (async_record, async_override, async_clear) are callbacks for this reason. In apply_lighting there’s no await between planning the writes and recording their claims, so no state change can land in between and be misjudged. (The async_ prefix is HA’s convention for “must run on the loop”, not “is a coroutine”.) .

27.title: Startup
27.content: sequenceDiagram autonumber participant HA as Home Assistant participant I as flare/__init__.py participant SE as Schedules entry participant ST as Settings entry participant FE as Flares entry HA->>I: async_setup (once per domain) Note over I: static path /flare_static/#lt;hash#gt;/,<br/>add_extra_js_url(loader),<br/>OldFingerprintView, FrontendLoadedView,<br/>export/import_schedule, resolve_target HA->>SE: async_setup_entry Note over SE: a ScheduleCoordinator per schedule,<br/>first refresh (defaults),<br/>forward 6 platforms,<br/>refresh again (restored values) HA->>ST: async_setup_entry Note over ST: ClaimRegistry.async_load (Store),<br/>claimed-light listeners,<br/>blueprint check at started,<br/>9 services, TickScheduler,<br/>forward sensor + button,<br/>release rooms restored dark,<br/>start area ticks HA->>FE: async_setup_entry Note over FE: forward light only if it has flares HA-->>HA: automations load (after integrations) HA-->>FE: EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_STARTED:<br/>each flare resolves its members HA-->>ST: async_at_started:<br/>check the blueprint . The order inside the Settings entry matters. | Claims load before the platforms, so the sensors start with them. | The services are registered before any platform, so nothing can call one that isn’t there yet. | The claim events start inside the sensor platform (ClaimEvents.start()). They seed every light’s status on the spot, which also notes the mismatch of a claim restored from before a restart. | Only after that are rooms restored dark released, so the release is announced in Activity. | The blueprint check waits for async_at_started: during setup no automation has loaded, so every blueprint looks unused. | . Flares wait for EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_STARTED for the same reason: automations load after integrations, so a flare can’t read its automation’s inputs until then.

28.title: Every hook
28.content: Bus listeners . | Listener | Where | Reacts by | . | each claimed light’s state | ClaimRegistry.async_start_listening, re-subscribed as the claimed set changes | dropping a claim when its light goes unavailable, releasing a room gone dark, noting mismatches | . | a light’s own state | each _LightStatusSensor | rewriting its status | . | a flare’s member lights | FlareLight, via async_track_target_selector_state_change_event | recomputing the group’s state | . | area_registry_updated | _tick_areas | handing the ticker the new set of areas | . | each claimed light’s registry entry | ClaimRegistry.async_start_listening, alongside its state listener | moving a claim with a rename; dropping it with a deletion | . | a light’s registry entry | each _LightStatusSensor | following a rename; removing the sensor when its light is deleted | . | an automation’s registry entry | each FlareLight, for its own automation | re-resolving its members when the automation is renamed or deleted | . | automation_reloaded | FlareLight | re-reading the automation’s lights | . | homeassistant_started | FlareLight | resolving its initial members once automations have loaded | . | homeassistant_stop | Settings entry, ClaimEvents | stopping the area ticker and cancelling pending timers | . Timers . | Timer | Interval | Where | . | Area tick | each area once per tick_interval minutes (default 1), tick_gap seconds apart (default 1) | TickScheduler, chaining async_track_point_in_utc_time | . | Schedule refresh | 60 s, plus on demand (debounced, at most 10 s) | ScheduleCoordinator (DataUpdateCoordinator) | . | Claims save | 5 s after a change, and at shutdown | Store.async_delay_save | . | Mismatch recheck | once, 31 s after a light first mismatches | ClaimEvents._recheck_after_grace | . | Controlled announcement | 3 s after a room’s first light is taken | ClaimEvents._controlled_soon | . There’s no polling of claim statuses. Everything that can move a count reaches the state listener: a drop, a light going off, one arriving, a mismatch starting or ending. The 30-second grace is the only change that time makes by itself, and it gets its own recheck. Signals . SIGNAL_CLAIMS_UPDATED (dispatcher) is how the registry tells everything showing claims to redraw: the count sensors, the status sensors, the Clear button’s tracked count, and _LightStatuses, which adds a status sensor the first time a room names a light. flowchart LR W["a write<br/>(async_record,<br/>override, clear)"] --> N L["state listener:<br/>drop / off / arrive /<br/>mismatch change"] --> N N["ClaimRegistry._notify()"] --> SAVE["Store.async_delay_save (5 s)"] N --> EV["ClaimEvents.async_claims_changed()<br/>→ refresh statuses, fire events"] N --> SIG["dispatcher:<br/>SIGNAL_CLAIMS_UPDATED"] SIG --> CS["count sensors"] SIG --> LS["status sensors"] SIG --> BT["Clear button"] SIG --> NEW["_LightStatuses:<br/>add sensors for new lights"] . ClaimEvents is reached directly, through the ClaimListener protocol, rather than by signal, because it must refresh before the sensors redraw. _notify() calls it first. It’s a protocol so tracking/ needn’t import sensor.py.

29.title: Contexts: telling FLARE’s writes apart
29.content: Every state change in HA carries a Context. A service call made with a context passes it to the entity, and the entity’s next state write carries it. Override protection is built on that. sequenceDiagram participant AU as Room automation run participant SV as flare.apply_lighting participant L as light.turn_on participant B as Bulb entity Note over AU: one Context per run (ctx A) AU->>SV: call (context: ctx A) SV->>SV: record claim: latest = ctx A, target SV->>L: light.turn_on (context: ctx A) L->>B: async_turn_on B-->>B: async_write_ha_state()<br/>new state's context = ctx A Note over B: within 5 s: context matches → "controlled"<br/>later reports: compare values with the target . Four facts shape everything built on contexts: . | One context per automation run. Every call in a run shares it, so context.user_id can’t tell FLARE’s write from another automation’s, but context.id can. | An entity forgets the context 5 seconds after the call. A slow bulb that reports later does so under a fresh context, with the values that were asked for. That’s why every claim also records its target, and a light matching the target by value counts as FLARE’s. | Two-step writes make child contexts. Brightness and colour go out as separate calls, each with its own Context(parent_id=...), created before the claims are recorded so both ids are in the claim. | A restart gives every light a new context. Restored claims can only ever match by value. | .

30.title: Ordering subtleties
30.content: . | The Phase event fires after the sensor updates. One coordinator refresh updates the schedule sensor and the Phase event entity. The event entity defers its fire with loop.call_soon, so an automation woken by it reads the sensor’s new phase, not the old one. That’s needed: HA starts the automation’s run inside the event entity’s own state write, so its variables: render before anything after it. | variables: render once, at trigger time. Nothing in the blueprint’s action: may delay, or later steps would act on a stale snapshot (see The room automation). | Claims are recorded before the write. A run cancelled part-way (mode: restart, a two-step bulb mid-sleep) still leaves the claim. A claim for a write that never lands does no harm: the light still matches its previous claim. | .

31.title: Shutdown
31.content: . | Any state a light reports while HA is stopping is ignored (hass.is_stopping). MQTT marks its lights unavailable as its connection closes, which would otherwise drop every claim just before the Store’s final write. | The Store writes once more at EVENT_HOMEASSISTANT_FINAL_WRITE, so a clean restart loses nothing. A crash loses at most the last 5 seconds, and FLARE fails open: a light without a claim is free to drive. | The ticker and ClaimEvents cancel their own timers on homeassistant_stop. Nothing unloads config entries at shutdown, and the tests fail on lingering timers. | .

32.title: Examples
32.content: When you want FLARE to behave differently some of the time, such as a later Morning at the weekend, or the house held at Night during a film, you don’t need a setting for it. Almost everything in FLARE is an ordinary Home Assistant entity or event, so an automation of your own can change it or react to it. Each example here is a complete automation to paste in and adjust. They use a schedule called Home, so its entities are time.home_…, number.home_…, sensor.home_flare, select.home_flare_phase, and event.home_flare_phase. Swap in your own schedule’s name, and your own rooms, lights and sensors. On this page . | A weekend lie-in | A holiday schedule | Movie night | Lighting a room from a remote | Lamps that follow a wall switch | Something else at a phase change | Being told when a light is taken over | .

33.title: A weekend lie-in
33.content: Morning starts later on Saturday and Sunday. alias: Weekend lie-in triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: event.home_flare_phase conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ trigger.to_state.attributes.event_type == 'Night' }}" actions: # Friday and Saturday nights set up a lie-in for the next morning; # every other night sets the weekday times back. - variables: lie_in: "{{ now().weekday() in [4, 5] }}" - action: time.set_value target: entity_id: time.home_morning_time data: time: "{{ '08:00:00' if lie_in else '06:00:00' }}" - action: time.set_value target: entity_id: time.home_day_time data: time: "{{ '09:30:00' if lie_in else '08:00:00' }}" . Changing Morning’s start time during Morning itself shifts today’s phase straight away, so the trick is to change it the night before. This automation runs when Night starts — after today’s morning, and before tomorrow’s. | It runs every night, not just at the weekend, so the weekday times come back on Sunday night without a second automation. | Day moves with Morning. Morning lasts until Day starts, so moving Morning to 08:00 while Day still starts at 08:00 would leave no Morning at all. | If your Night starts after midnight, use [5, 6]: by then it’s already Saturday. | .

34.title: A holiday schedule
34.content: Switch the whole house to a holiday schedule, with later mornings and later nights, from a toggle, and back again when the holiday’s over. First create a Toggle helper called Holiday mode (Settings → Devices & Services → Helpers → Create helper → Toggle). Then: . alias: Holiday schedule triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: input_boolean.holiday_mode actions: - if: "{{ is_state('input_boolean.holiday_mode', 'on') }}" then: - action: flare.import_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" schedule: | morning: time: "08:30" day: time: "10:00" night: time: "23:30" else: - action: flare.import_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" schedule: | morning: time: "06:00" day: time: "08:00" night: time: "22:00" . Each YAML block lists only the settings that change; everything else keeps its current value. A schedule can hold any of its settings, so for bigger changes, set your schedule up the way you want it, press Copy in its dashboard section, and paste the result in.

35.title: Movie night
35.content: Hold the house at Night while the TV is on, and hand back to the schedule when it goes off. alias: Movie night triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: media_player.living_room_tv to: playing id: start - trigger: state entity_id: media_player.living_room_tv from: playing id: stop actions: - action: select.select_option target: entity_id: select.home_flare_phase data: option: "{{ 'Night' if trigger.id == 'start' else 'Auto' }}" . The phase override applies to every room on that schedule. To dim one room only, give it a schedule of its own, or use the blueprint’s Brightness Template instead.

36.title: Lighting a room from a remote
36.content: Turn the hall lights on from a button on a remote, at the right level for the time of day. alias: Hall lights from the remote triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: event.hall_remote_action conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ trigger.to_state.attributes.event_type == 'on' }}" actions: - action: automation.trigger target: entity_id: automation.hallway_lights . If the hall has a flare, you can turn that on instead, like any other light. It runs the room’s automation in the same way: . actions: - action: light.turn_on target: entity_id: light.hallway_lights_flare .

37.title: Lamps that follow a wall switch
37.content: The living room has smart bulbs in its pendants, on an ordinary wall switch, and smart lamps around the room. Switching the pendants off at the wall cuts their power, so Home Assistant sees them go unavailable rather than off. Switching on needs nothing extra. When you switch the pendants on at the wall, they come back online lit, so the room counts as in use and FLARE sets the pendants to the curve and turns the lamps on with them. Switching off needs an automation of its own, because FLARE doesn’t turn the lamps off when the pendants lose power: . alias: Living room lamps off with the pendants triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: - light.living_room_pendant_1 - light.living_room_pendant_2 to: unavailable actions: - action: light.turn_off target: entity_id: - light.living_room_lamp_1 - light.living_room_lamp_2 . If you’d rather leave the lamps to another automation or a voice assistant, so FLARE never switches them on or off, hand them over with a null level, as in Leaving a light alone.

38.title: Something else at a phase change
38.content: Close the blinds when Night starts. alias: Blinds at Night triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: event.home_flare_phase conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ trigger.to_state.attributes.event_type == 'Night' }}" actions: - action: cover.close_cover target: area_id: living_room . The Phase event fires each time the phase changes, including a manual override, with the new phase as its event_type.

39.title: Being told when a light is taken over
39.content: A notification when FLARE stops driving a light because something else changed it. alias: Tell me when FLARE lets go of a light triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_light_overridden actions: - action: notify.notify data: message: > {{ state_attr(trigger.event.data.light, 'friendly_name') }} was changed by something else, so FLARE has stopped driving it until the room goes dark. The event also carries what FLARE last asked for and what the light was actually showing — see FLARE’s events.

40.title: Flares
40.content: A flare is a light entity that sits over an automation. Flares are under Settings → Devices & Services → FLARE → Flares. For setting one up for a voice assistant, see Voice assistants. On this page . | Settings | The flare’s light | Flares and the room’s automation | .

41.title: Settings
41.content: | Setting | Description | . | Automation | The automation that turning the flare on runs. If the automation is deleted, the flare becomes unavailable. | . | Name | The flare’s display name (and what voice assistants hear). Renaming it later doesn’t change its entity ID. | . | Lights input | For an automation built from a blueprint: the input that holds the lights. The flare reads that input whenever it’s used, so changing the automation updates the flare. For an automation from the FLARE blueprint this is Lights & Occupancy. | . | Lights | For an automation not built from a blueprint: the lights, picked directly. | . | Area | Shown only when adding a flare for another automation: the area the flare’s device starts in, defaulting to the automation’s area. Afterwards, change the device’s area the usual way in Home Assistant. | . Set up area offers a flare for each area it sets up, named after the area. Adding flares from Rooms from the FLARE blueprint creates a flare for each room picked, named after its automation. In both cases, the new flare is placed in its automation’s area. Reconfigure flare (in the flare’s three-dot menu) shows which automation the flare runs, and lets you change its Name and either its Lights or Lights input. It can’t switch a flare to a different automation — add a new flare if you need that.

42.title: The flare’s light
42.content: light.<name>_flare reports the combined state of its lights, as a Home Assistant light group does: on if any of them is on, with their average brightness and colour. Its entity_id attribute lists the lights. | Call | What it does | . | light.turn_on with no brightness, colour or effect | Runs the automation, as Run actions does. A transition on its own is ignored. | . | light.turn_on with a brightness, colour or effect | Marks every light as overridden for that automation’s room via flare.claims_override, then sends the values to the lights as a light group does. FLARE leaves them alone until the room is empty and dark. | . | light.turn_off | Marks every light as overridden in the same way, then turns them off. They stay off until the room’s automation next turns them on, such as when it detects motion. | . For an automation built from a blueprint, the flare’s lights match the automation’s target as described under Room. A light that belongs to another flare is always excluded.

43.title: Flares and the room’s automation
43.content: A flare’s own light is never one of a room’s lights: the FLARE blueprint and FLARE’s services skip it, even when it sits in the room’s area.

44.title: Voice assistants
44.content: If you say “Hey Siri, turn on the kitchen”, Siri switches the kitchen’s bulbs on directly. They come on at whatever brightness and colour they had last, and because FLARE didn’t set them, they read as overridden and FLARE leaves them alone until the room goes dark. The same happens with Alexa, Google, HomeKit scenes and dashboard buttons. A flare avoids this. It’s a light, light.kitchen_flare, that you give to your voice assistant or the Home app instead of the bulbs. Turning it on runs the kitchen’s FLARE automation, so the room comes on at the right brightness and colour for the time of day and FLARE keeps adjusting it from there. Dimming it or turning it off sets every light in the room, as the table under What each command does shows. On this page . | Adding flares for your rooms . | Name it the way you’ll say it | . | What each command does | Exposing flares instead of your bulbs . | HomeKit | Alexa and Google Assistant | Assist | . | A flare for your own automation | .

45.title: Adding flares for your rooms
45.content: After setting up areas with Set up area, including when you first add FLARE, choose Pick rooms for flares. Every room you just set up is listed and ticked, and each room you keep ticked gets a flare named after its area. For a room automation you made yourself, go to Settings → Devices & Services → FLARE → Add flare and choose Rooms from the FLARE blueprint. Every room automation that doesn’t have a flare yet is listed and ticked, so you can add a flare for every room at once, or untick the ones you don’t want. Each one is named after its automation. A flare is placed in its automation’s area and appears as light.<name>_flare. It always tracks the same lights as its room’s automation, so when your automation targets an area, floor, or label, any new bulb you add to that room joins the flare automatically. Name it the way you’ll say it . A flare’s name is what Siri, Alexa and Google hear. Automations often have names like “Kitchen lighting” or “Garden Lights Adaptive”, which nobody says out loud. If a flare was named after an automation like that, rename it to the room’s plain name — such as “Kitchen” or “Garden” — using Reconfigure flare in the flare’s three-dot menu. Renaming a flare doesn’t change its entity ID. If the flare is already in the Home app or the Alexa app, rename it there too, because they can keep the name they first saw.

46.title: What each command does
46.content: | You say or tap | What happens | . | “Turn on the kitchen” | The room’s automation runs, and the room comes on the way it normally would. | . | “Set the kitchen to 30%”, or a colour | Every light in the room is set to that. FLARE leaves them there until the room is empty and dark. | . | “Turn on the kitchen” again | The room goes back to FLARE: the automation runs, and every light returns to the curve. | . | “Turn off the kitchen” | Every light in the room turns off, and stays off until the room’s sensors next detect motion. | .

47.title: Exposing flares instead of your bulbs
47.content: Expose each room’s flare and stop exposing its bulbs. If you expose both, every room shows up twice, and “turn on the kitchen” may go to the bulbs, which come on at whatever they last had instead of following the room. The bulbs keep working in Home Assistant either way. HomeKit . FLARE names every flare light.<name>_flare, so if your HomeKit Bridge is set up in YAML, one pattern exports every flare, including ones you add later: . homekit: filter: include_entity_globs: - light.*_flare . Leave out include_domains: light if you have it, or the bulbs are exported as well. Home Assistant reads this when it starts, so restart after changing it. If you set the bridge up from the UI instead, use Configure on the HomeKit Bridge integration, choose to include entities, and pick the flares. HomeKit doesn’t use Home Assistant’s areas, so put each flare in its room in the Home app. If the bridge used to export your bulbs, they stay in the Home app as “Not Responding” until you remove the bridge from the Home app and pair it again. Alexa and Google Assistant . With Home Assistant Cloud, go to Settings → Voice assistants → Expose, expose the flares and un-expose the bulbs. If Expose new entities is on, the flares are already exposed, but so is every bulb. Google Assistant puts each flare in the room matching its Home Assistant area. Alexa doesn’t use areas, so put each flare in a group for its room in the Alexa app. If you set up exposure in YAML instead, the same include_entity_globs pattern works in the filter: under cloud: alexa:, cloud: google_actions: and a manual alexa: smart_home:. A manual google_assistant: setup has no filter, so expose the flares there with entity_config instead. Assist . Assist uses the same Expose list. Expose the flares and un-expose the bulbs, and “turn on the kitchen” turns on the flare. If you’d rather keep the flare’s name as it is, add the room’s name as an alias on the flare instead, under Voice assistants in its settings.

48.title: A flare for your own automation
48.content: Any automation can have a flare. Choose Another automation when adding one: . | If the automation is built from a blueprint, pick the input that holds its lights. | If it isn’t built from a blueprint, pick its lights directly. | . When you change brightness or colour from a flare, or turn it off, the flare marks those lights as overridden. For your own automation to respect that override instead of resetting the lights on its next update, its calls to flare.apply_lighting must pass a room (room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}"). Without room_id, flare.apply_lighting doesn’t check overrides at all. Turning the flare on runs that automation. The other commands work the same as above. The Flares reference lists every setting.

49.title: How flares work
49.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. A flare (light.<name>_flare) is a light that fronts a room automation, so a voice assistant, HomeKit or a dashboard can switch a room without going around it. Saying “turn the kitchen on” to Siri goes to the flare, and the flare runs the kitchen’s automation. Siri’s own “on” sent straight to the bulbs would read as an override, and the room would be left at whatever the bulbs restored to.

50.title: What it is in code
50.content: FlareLight (light.py) subclasses HA’s own LightGroup, so state, brightness and colour are the group’s, worked out from its members. Two things differ from a plain light group: who its members are, and what “on” means. flowchart LR sub["Flares entry subentry<br/>{automation: registry id,<br/>lights_input: room_target}"] --> inst["FlareInstance"] inst --> fl["FlareLight<br/>(LightGroup)"] auto["automation entity<br/>_blueprint_inputs"] -->|"lights_target()"| tgt["target<br/>{area_id: kitchen}"] tgt -->|"async_track_target_selector_<br/>state_change_event"| mem["members:<br/>the room's lights, minus flares"] mem --> fl . Membership . A flare stores two things: its automation, by entity-registry id so a rename doesn’t orphan it, and the name of the input holding the room’s lights (room_target for our blueprint). It reads the input’s value live. A plain automation, not made from a blueprint, stores a target instead. | The inputs come from the automation entity’s private _blueprint_inputs (flares/automation.py:blueprint_inputs). Its raw_config is the substituted config, so it doesn’t have them. This is an accepted risk, kept to that one function, and the behaviour tests break if HA changes it. | Members are tracked with async_track_target_selector_state_change_event, HA’s own target resolution: the same rule as flare.resolve_target, so a flare’s members are exactly its room’s lights. | It re-resolves on automation_reloaded, on entity-registry changes to automations, and once at homeassistant_started (automations load after integrations). | A flare is never one of a room’s lights. 67.title: FLARE
67.content: Flexible Lighting Automation & Reconciliation Engine — phase-based circadian lighting for Home Assistant, with scene handoff and override protection built in. Quickstart (5 mins) Curve playground GitHub .

68.title: What it does
68.content: FLARE sets your lights through the day, and leaves alone any light you change yourself. | It lights the room when you walk in. With a motion or occupancy sensor, the room comes on at the right brightness and colour for the time of day, or in the scene you’ve picked for it, and turns off once it’s empty. | It works with lights on a physical wall switch. If you cut the power to a room and restore it, FLARE sets each bulb to the current brightness and colour as soon as it shows up in Home Assistant again, instead of leaving it at whatever it powered up as. | It keeps every light on the curve. Every minute it checks each light, and corrects any that have drifted or missed a command. | Each room can be different. Give a light its own brightness, hand the room to a scene in any phase, or use a template when a fixed value isn’t enough. | It can leave a nightlight on. When a room empties it can dim to a low level instead of going dark. | It leaves your changes alone. If you change a light yourself, from an app, a wall switch or another automation, FLARE stops setting it until the room next goes dark. | It works with Siri, Alexa and Google. Each room gets a single light to expose to them, so “turn on the kitchen” lights the kitchen at the right brightness and colour for the time of day, rather than at whatever the bulbs were last set to. If you ask for a specific brightness or colour, FLARE leaves those lights alone until the room goes dark. | It’s gentle on your Zigbee network. Rooms update one after another rather than all at once, and changes too small to see aren’t sent. | .

69.title: Setting it up
69.content: Adding FLARE creates your schedules and can set up an automation for each room with lights; afterwards you can add the dashboard in Home Assistant. The Quickstart goes through it step by step.

70.title: Four phases, not one curve
70.content: Most adaptive lighting follows the sun’s position. That means evening lighting at 4pm in winter, and bright light until 9pm in summer, whatever time you actually get up and go to bed. FLARE works from your schedule instead, dividing the day into four named phases. With the default settings: . | Phase | What it’s for | . | Morning | Bright and cold — enough eyeball caffeine to get you as far as the coffee machine, with some research to back it up. | . | Day | Bright, easing steadily from Morning’s colour toward Evening’s across the whole afternoon. | . | Evening | Dimmer and warmer, anchored to your actual sunset. | . | Night | Warm and low overnight, easing into Morning before dawn. | . Each boundary has its own transition: how long beforehand to start easing into the next phase, so the new values land exactly as it begins. If you set a transition to zero, the lights step straight to the new values instead. Morning, Day and Night start at fixed times of day. Only Evening tracks the sun, and it’s kept between an earliest and a latest time, so it moves with the season without drifting into the small hours. Play with the curve to see how each setting shapes the day.

71.title: Home Assistant native
71.content: Every schedule setting is an ordinary Home Assistant entity, and the room automation is an ordinary automation, so when a default isn’t what you want, you change it with the tools you already use. For example: . | A weekend lie-in, by an automation that moves Morning later on Friday and Saturday evenings. | A holiday schedule, switched on and off with a toggle. | A room lit by a button on a remote, not just by occupancy. | Blinds that close when Night starts. | . 75.content: FLARE’s setup asks: . | Your schedules. A schedule is the day’s lighting: when each phase starts, and how bright and warm it is. One for the whole home (called Home) is the default, and enough for most homes. 85.title: Override protection
85.content: FLARE records what it last asked each light for, so it can tell its own changes from anyone else’s and leave alone a light you’ve changed yourself. Its entities and options are under Settings → Devices & Services → FLARE → Settings. For what override protection means for your lights day to day, see the Override protection guide.
