86.title: FLARE’s entities
86.content: | Entity | Description | . | sensor.flare_controlled_lights | The number of lights FLARE is setting. For information only. | . | sensor.flare_overridden_lights | The number of lights something else has changed. For information only. | . | button.flare_clear | Discards every claim. | . | sensor.<light>_flare_status | Created for each light targeted by a room automation, on the light’s own device: holds its status. Its attributes list light (the light entity ID), rooms (the rooms it belongs to), claimed (whether FLARE holds a claim on it), asked (what FLARE last asked it for), confirmed (the older claim FLARE last saw the light take — see two claims, not one), and differs (which fields don’t match within the tolerances: state, brightness, or color). | . The two counts and each light’s status are recorded in history, with long-term statistics for the counts. asked, confirmed, and differs aren’t recorded, since they change with every update. A light that is unavailable or has no claim isn’t included in either count. The dashboard also shows the house-wide totals and the lights for each area. FLARE keeps its claims in Home Assistant’s own storage, so they’re kept across a restart. To see every claim at once, download the diagnostics from FLARE → Settings: they list each light’s claims and each room’s lights. They also list the last 50 overrides, each with what FLARE asked for, what the light reported and what kind of light it is. A light’s status sensor is created the first time a room automation runs with that light, under Diagnostic on the light’s device page, and stays even after the room releases the light. The status sensor becomes unavailable whenever the light itself is unavailable, and is deleted automatically if the light is removed. If a light has no device (such as a light group), FLARE creates a standalone status sensor named <Light name> FLARE status instead. An automation can trigger on the status sensor: . triggers: - trigger: state entity_id: sensor.kitchen_1_flare_status to: overridden . Clear discards every claim, not only for the overridden lights. FLARE then sets every light again on its next update.

87.title: How it works
87.content: FLARE tells a light you’ve changed from one it set by keeping a record of what it last asked each light for, and comparing the light against that record. Claims . Each time FLARE sets a light, it records a claim holding what it asked the light for. On every update, FLARE compares each light against its claim to determine its status: . | controlled — The light matches its claim, so updates keep moving it along the curve. | mismatched — The light stopped matching less than 30 seconds ago. FLARE leaves it alone while waiting for slow bulbs to finish reporting back, without counting or announcing it as overridden yet. | overridden — The light hasn’t matched its claim for at least 30 seconds, so updates leave it alone. | untracked — The light is on with no confirmed claim yet, so FLARE sets it and records a claim. | . (See Inspecting tracked state for the complete table of all six statuses, including off and unavailable.) . “Matches” means within a tolerance, since bulbs rarely report back exactly what they were sent — 5% of the brightness and 5 mireds of the colour temperature by default. See how close counts as a match. Example: dimming a lamp . The living room has a ceiling light and a lamp, and someone’s in the room. | Time | What happens | The lamp’s claim | The lamp | Status | . | 19:00 | FLARE sets the room | on, 180, 3000 K | on, 180, 3000 K | controlled | . | 19:20 | You dim the lamp in the Home app | on, 180, 3000 K | on, 60, 3000 K | mismatched | . | 19:20:30 |   | on, 180, 3000 K | on, 60, 3000 K | overridden | . | 19:21 | FLARE’s next update | on, 180, 3000 K | on, 60, 3000 K | overridden | . | 23:00 | You switch both lights off | deleted | off | off | . | 07:00 | Motion in the morning | on, 255, 6667 K | on, 255, 6667 K | controlled | . From 19:21 the update keeps setting the ceiling light to the curve, but leaves the lamp out, because it’s overridden. So the lamp stays at 60 all evening. At 23:00 none of the room’s lights is on, so the room deletes their claims (see how a light goes back to the curve). While off with no claim, the lamp’s status is off. When morning motion arrives and turns the room on, FLARE sets the lamp to the curve and records a new controlled claim. Example: switching a lamp off . Switching a light off counts as changing it, the same as dimming it. With the same room: . | Time | What happens | The lamp’s claim | The lamp | Status | . | 19:00 | FLARE sets the room | on, 180, 3000 K | on, 180, 3000 K | controlled | . | 20:00 | You switch the lamp off | on, 180, 3000 K | off | mismatched | . | 20:00:30 |   | on, 180, 3000 K | off | overridden | . | 20:01 | FLARE’s next update | on, 180, 3000 K | off | overridden | . The ceiling light is still on, so the room keeps its claims, and every update leaves the lamp off. Once you switch the ceiling light off too, the room deletes both claims, and both lights come on next time. Lights FLARE switches off . When FLARE switches a light off itself, it sets the light’s claim to off first. The light then matches its claim, so it’s controlled rather than overridden, and it comes on again with the rest of the room. That happens when: . | a light’s brightness level is 0, such as a light excluded in the current phase, | a room empties and Idle Brightness leaves a nightlight on, and the room’s other lights are switched off. | . In that second case the nightlight keeps the room from going dark, so the room keeps its claims. Because the other lights’ claims say off, they come on when someone walks back in. If your own automation switches lights off, the flare.turn_off or light.turn_off comparison shows which to use. Back to the curve . An overridden light goes back to the curve once its claim is gone, or once FLARE sets it regardless: . | The room goes dark. Once none of the room’s claimed lights is on, the room deletes all their claims. A light that’s unavailable counts as off, so one dead bulb can’t hold a room’s claims forever. A light in the room that FLARE has no claim on (such as a lamp run by another automation) neither holds the room open when on nor blocks release. | You press Clear. Clear under FLARE → Settings, or an area’s Clear on the dashboard, deletes claims, so FLARE sets those lights at its next update. | You run the room’s automation yourself, or turn on the room’s flare with no brightness or colour. That sets every light, overridden ones included, and records new claims. | The light goes unavailable. Its claim is deleted, so it starts unclaimed (untracked if on, or off if off) when it comes back online, and FLARE sets it again. | . A restart doesn’t send a light back: claims are kept across restarts, and a light still showing what its claim says is still controlled. When a room’s lights come back online together, such as when they’re switched on at the wall, FLARE waits a few seconds before setting them. A bulb starts up at whatever it powers up as and misses a command sent while it boots, which would leave it not matching its claim. Two claims, not one . Each light actually has two claims: the last thing FLARE sent it, and the last thing FLARE saw it show. A light matching either one is controlled. So if a command never reaches a bulb, such as a dropped Zigbee message, the bulb still matches the older claim and isn’t counted as overridden. FLARE sends the command again at its next update. What the services record . flare.apply_lighting records a claim on each light it sets when given a room_id, and flare.turn_off updates the claim of each light it switches off to off. When flare.apply_lighting is called with a room_id, any on light with no claim is sent the target values even if the light is already showing them, so that write establishes a claim on the light. After pressing Clear, for example, a room’s lit lights are claimed again on their next update. By contrast, when flare.apply_lighting is called without a room_id, nothing is sent to lights that already show the target values, and no claims are recorded. Rooms . Claims belong to the lights, not to any one automation, so two automations setting the same light don’t count each other’s changes as overrides. Each room automation names its lights, and that’s what decides which claims are deleted together when the room goes dark. If a light is in two rooms, its claim is deleted when either room goes dark. Each call that records claims names a room, usually the automation making it, and the room’s lights. The blueprint passes its own automation as room_id and its Lights & Occupancy lights as room_entities. If you call the services yourself, do the same: . action: flare.apply_lighting data: entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] brightness: 200 color_temp_kelvin: 3200 transition: 2 room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" room_entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2, light.kitchen_lamp] . | Without room_id, apply_lighting sets the lights without recording any claims, and doesn’t skip overridden lights. | turn_off doesn’t take a room: it updates only the lights FLARE already holds claims on, keeping them in whichever rooms they already belong to. | claims_record and claims_override require room_id. claims_check and claims_clear don’t take one. | Without room_entities, a room’s lights are whichever lights its calls have set. | force: true sets lights even if something else has changed them, and records the claim. | An unclaimed light is free for FLARE to set, so if your own automation turns on or adjusts an unclaimed light, FLARE will overwrite it unless you mark it with flare.claims_override. | . If an automation is renamed, FLARE keeps tracking its room continuously. If an automation is deleted, its room is removed along with it, and FLARE releases the claims on any lights that no other room drives. How close counts as a match . A light matches a claim’s values if it’s within a tolerance of them, so only a change you’d notice counts as someone else’s. Bulbs rarely report back exactly what they were sent: a colour temperature asked for as 4294 K can come back as 4312 K. You can set the tolerances under FLARE → Settings → Configure: . | Option | Default | Description | . | Brightness tolerance | 5% | How far, as a percentage of the brightness FLARE asked for, a light’s brightness can be and still match. A dim light always gets at least 2 (of 255). | . | Colour temperature tolerance | 5 mireds | How far a light’s colour temperature can be from what FLARE asked for and still match. For a light set by RGB, the red, green and blue differences added together can be up to twice this (10 by default). That includes a light with no colour temperature of its own, such as an RGB LED strip, which Home Assistant sets to the RGB for the colour temperature FLARE asks for. | . The same tolerances decide what’s worth sending: if a light is already within the tolerances of its target, FLARE doesn’t send it a command. If lights are marked overridden when nobody has changed them, look at the difference shown on the dashboard and raise the matching tolerance (Brightness tolerance or Colour temperature tolerance). Lower the tolerances if you want FLARE to catch smaller manual changes.

88.title: FLARE’s events
88.content: FLARE fires events when a room takes control of lights, when it releases them, and when something else overrides a light. Each event is filed under one of FLARE’s entities (its Controlled lights or Overridden lights count, or Clear for a release) on FLARE’s service device, so they appear in FLARE’s Activity. room names the automation. Normal updates to lights FLARE is already controlling aren’t announced. When a room starts controlling lights it wasn’t driving before (such as when the room turns on), FLARE waits 3 seconds so bulbs reporting back one by one can be grouped together, then fires flare_lights_controlled: . lights: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] # the lights it took controlled: 6 # how many of its lights FLARE is controlling now room: automation.kitchen_lighting entity_id: sensor.flare_controlled_lights device_id: ... # FLARE's device . Kitchen Lighting is now controlling 6 lights . When a room lets its lights go, because it went dark or you pressed Clear, FLARE fires flare_lights_released: . lights: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] room: automation.kitchen_lighting entity_id: button.flare_clear device_id: ... Kitchen Lighting cleared 6 lights . When something else changes one of FLARE’s lights, and it stays changed for 30 seconds, FLARE fires flare_light_overridden for that light: . light: light.kitchen_1 rooms: [automation.kitchen_lighting] # every room it belongs to entity_id: sensor.flare_overridden_lights device_id: ... previous_status: controlled live_context_id: 01M11... live: { state: on, brightness: 12, color_temp_kelvin: 6500 } # or rgb_color, for a colour observed: { context_id: ..., target: {...}, recorded_at: ... } latest: { context_id: ..., target: {...}, recorded_at: ... } . Kitchen Lighting released Kitchen 1 to something else (last asked for 255/6667, found 12/6500) . live shows the state the light reported: its brightness and colour temperature, or its rgb_color if it wasn’t showing a white or doesn’t support colour temperature. When a colour temperature light reports xy_color for a white shade, FLARE converts that into color_temp_kelvin. flare_light_overridden fires once when a light becomes overridden, doesn’t repeat while it stays overridden, and doesn’t re-fire on startup for lights that were already overridden before a restart. To trigger an automation on it: . triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_light_overridden .

89.title: Inspecting tracked state
89.content: flare.claims_check returns each light’s status, and each light’s status sensor shows it: . | Status | Meaning | . | controlled | FLARE is setting it: it matches one of its claims. | . | overridden | It has matched neither claim for at least 30 seconds, so something else has changed it. | . | mismatched | It has matched neither claim for less than 30 seconds. Usually FLARE’s own command is still taking effect, or a light that just came back online is still reporting its old values, so FLARE leaves it alone meanwhile without counting or announcing it as overridden yet. | . | untracked | It’s on, and either has no claim or only an unconfirmed first claim that the light hasn’t reported back for yet. FLARE sets it as usual. | . | off | It’s off and has no claim. A light FLARE turned off is controlled; a light someone else turned off is overridden. | . | unavailable | Home Assistant can’t reach it, so its claims aren’t checked and FLARE skips it. | . matched_via says which claim matched, and how: latest-context, latest-value, observed-context or observed-value. rooms lists the rooms the light belongs to. Each claim records a recorded_at timestamp and a context_id, which you can use to trace the change in Home Assistant’s logbook. A light’s claim moves with it when the entity is renamed, and is deleted if the light is removed from Home Assistant.

90.title: When rooms update
90.content: FLARE fires a flare_tick event for each area once per update interval, carrying the area as area_id. Areas tick one after another in name order, spaced apart by the configured gap, so rooms don’t all send commands at the same time. A tick is a plain event, not an entity, so it never appears in Activity, history or the logbook. You can set the interval and the gap under FLARE → Settings → Configure (alongside the matching tolerances and Two-step bulb models): . | Option | Default | Description | . | Update interval | 1 minute | How often each area ticks, from 1 to 60 minutes. | . | Gap between areas | 1 second | Reduced automatically when the areas wouldn’t otherwise fit in the interval. | . A room automation from the blueprint follows the tick of the first area in its Lights & Occupancy. To run your own automation on an area’s tick: . triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_tick event_data: area_id: kitchen .

91.title: Override protection
91.content: Without override protection, a lamp you dim to read by would be set straight back to the curve at FLARE’s next update, within a minute. With it, FLARE leaves a light you’ve changed yourself alone until the whole room has been dark. For how FLARE tells your changes from its own, see Override protection in the reference. On this page . | What override protection is . | What counts as changing a light | What it doesn’t do | . | Back to the curve | Seeing what’s going on | Turning it off for a room | .

92.title: What override protection is
92.content: FLARE sets each room’s lights to the curve at every update, every minute by default. Once you’ve changed a light, it’s overridden, and FLARE’s updates leave it as you set it while the rest of the room carries on following the curve. Once every light in the room is off, FLARE sets all of them again the next time the room comes on. For example, you dim the reading lamp at 20:00. All evening the ceiling light keeps following the curve, getting warmer and dimmer, while the lamp stays at your brightness. At bedtime you switch everything off, and in the morning the lamp comes on with the rest of the room, set to the curve. What counts as changing a light . Anything other than FLARE changing a light’s brightness, its colour, or whether it’s on: . | a wall switch or a remote, | the Home Assistant app, or another app such as Hue or HomeKit, | a voice assistant, | another automation, script or scene. | . Switching a light off counts too, so a lamp you’ve switched off stays off while the rest of the room is lit, rather than coming back on at the next update. A change too small to notice doesn’t count, since bulbs rarely report back exactly what they were sent. See how close counts as a match. What it doesn’t do . | It doesn’t stop a room switching off when it empties. Once every sensor has been clear for the Wait Time, the room’s lights go off, including ones you’ve changed. | It doesn’t last forever. It ends once the room has been dark, or when you press Clear. See how a light goes back to the curve. | It doesn’t affect lights FLARE isn’t running, such as a lamp left out of the room’s lights. | . Override protection is on for every room by default. To turn it off for a room, see turning it off for a room.

93.title: Back to the curve
93.content: An overridden light goes back to the curve when: . | the room goes dark: once every light FLARE is running in the room is off, the next time the room comes on, FLARE sets all of them again, | you press Clear, under FLARE → Settings or for an area on the dashboard, so FLARE sets those lights at its next update, | you run the room’s automation yourself, or turn on the room’s flare with no brightness or colour. | . A restart doesn’t send a light back. The reference has the details, such as what happens to a light that goes unavailable.

94.title: Seeing what’s going on
94.content: . | Each light controlled by a room automation has a FLARE status sensor on its device page, showing its status, what FLARE last asked it for, and what doesn’t match. | The dashboard’s Overrides view lists every area’s lights with the same details, and a Clear button for each light. | FLARE’s Activity shows when a room starts controlling its lights, when it lets them go, and when a light is overridden. | . Override protection in the reference lists the entities, events and options.

95.title: Turning it off for a room
95.content: If a room’s bulbs report values that don’t match what they actually show, FLARE can repeatedly mark them as overridden. First try raising the matching tolerances under FLARE → Settings → Configure (see how close counts as a match). If that still isn’t enough, you can turn off Override Protection in that room’s automation: every update will then set any light that isn’t showing the curve. See Turning override protection off for the full details.

97.title: The room automation
97.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. custom_components/flare/blueprints/flare.yaml is the blueprint each room automation is made from. It decides when a room updates and whether a light may come on. The services decide how: what to send, to which bulbs, and which lights to leave alone.

98.title: Why the split falls where it does
98.content: A condition: can’t call a service. So anything a condition needs has to be a template or a native condition, and that keeps triggers, conditions and occupancy in the blueprint. Anything that needs HA’s registries properly (which lights are the room’s), or is fiddly enough to want unit tests (grouping, override protection), is a service the blueprint calls in its action:. flowchart LR subgraph YAML["Blueprint (Jinja/YAML)"] tr["triggers"] co["the one top-level condition"] va["variables: occupancy, levels,<br/>idle, scenes, allow_turn_on"] ch["choose: off / self-heal / default"] end subgraph PY["Integration (Python)"] rt["flare.resolve_target"] sc["flare.compute_scene_coverage"] al["flare.apply_lighting"] to["flare.turn_off"] cc["flare.claims_clear"] end tr --> co --> rt --> va --> ch ch --> sc ch --> al ch --> to ch --> cc .

99.title: Triggers
99.content: | id | Fires on | Notes | . | phase_change | the schedule’s Phase event entity | a real phase change, and once after setup | . | tick | flare_tick with this room’s tick_area | the curve moves within a phase | . | tick | time_pattern every minute | only when the room names no area, chosen by enabled: | . | extra | Additional Trigger Entities (deprecated) | any state change of entities the user picked | . | motion_on | occupancy.detected, motion.detected | native triggers over room_target | . | motion_off | occupancy.cleared, motion.cleared, held for Wait time | per sensor | . | recovered | template: some room light reachable, held 5 s | all the room’s lights were unreachable and one is back | . | lux_dark | template: the room stops reading too bright (some illuminance sensor at or below Lux Threshold) | a wake-up only; the action re-checks | . | additional | Additional Triggers, the user’s own, last | by position: trigger_id is additional for any trigger at position 10 or later, whatever its own id | . The blueprint reads which trigger ran from trigger_id, never trigger.id: a user’s trigger can carry any id, motion_on included, and must never count as one of the blueprint’s own. trigger_variables: are the only variables available inside a trigger, so tick_area is computed there as the first area_id in room_target. Because trigger templates are limited and cannot call helpers like area_devices(), the recovered and lux_dark triggers expand room_target inline in Jinja. That expansion is close enough for a wake-up trigger, and once the automation runs, the action always resolves entities properly with flare.resolve_target.

So order matters, and the chain reads like this: . flowchart LR room["room.entities"] --> res["resolved_entities<br/>(lights, minus flares)"] room --> occ["room_occupancy_entities<br/>(working sensors)"] room --> lux["room_lux_entities"] --> tb["too_bright"] --> lb["lux_blocked_entities"] res --> bl["brightness_levels<br/>(exclude lists + template)"] --> ho["hands_off_entities<br/>(null / false)"] res --> ib["idle_brightness"] --> ie["idle_entities"] ho --> ie lb --> ie occ --> ocw["occupancy_clear_for_wait"] ie --> idle["room_is_idle"] occ --> idle ocw --> idle res --> occd["occupied<br/>(any light on)"] occd --> atl["allow_turn_on"] ocw --> atl tb --> atl . The gate . Exactly two things can switch a light on, scene.turn_on and flare.apply_lighting, and both sit inside one if allow_turn_on block in default:. allow_turn_on = manual_run or trigger.id == 'motion_on' or occupied # a light in the room is already on or (trigger.id == 'lux_dark' and not too_bright and someone is in the room) . It must never gain a new way to become true without the user asking for it explicitly. test_no_trigger_reaching_default_can_light_a_dark_empty_room sweeps every trigger against it. The one exception is idle brightness, the nightlight: an empty room settles to its idle levels outside the gate. It’s gated on room_is_idle instead, and the curve’s gate is allow_turn_on and not room_is_idle. Without that, an idle light being on would make occupied true, and the next tick would ramp the nightlight straight back up. Why there’s no delay anywhere in action: . Variables are a snapshot taken when the run starts. A delay before acting would act on that snapshot. A 0–15 s jitter delay once relit a light switched off by hand inside the window, because the run had already decided the room was in use. test_nothing_delays_the_action_before_it_decides pins it. A trigger’s own for: (as recovered and motion_off have) isn’t a delay in this sense, because the run, and so its variables, starts after it.

102.title: Occupancy details
102.content: . | room_occupancy_entities exists so the blueprint can tell whether the room has any working sensors at all. Home Assistant’s occupancy.is_detected condition returns false when given zero entities, so without this guard a lights-only room would always look empty. | Unavailable and unknown sensors are filtered out, so a room whose only sensor is offline is treated as sensorless rather than empty. | occupancy_clear_for_wait is computed with an explicit now() - last_changed check rather than relying on a native for: condition, because for: depends on recorder priming after a restart and is not always reliable. | When Sensors From Areas is off, the native occupancy and motion triggers still fire for every sensor in the target (since a trigger’s target: cannot take templates), so the top-level condition: drops events from sensors that weren’t picked directly by entity ID. | Any sensor excluded via Exclude target (Home Assistant 2026.11+) never fires the native triggers and is omitted by flare.resolve_target, so the blueprint needs no custom exclusion logic for them. Only the lux_dark and recovered Jinja wake-up triggers ignore exclusions, because they expand the target manually. | .

103.title: Scene handoff
103.content: If you’ve already made a scene for how a room should look at night, or while you’re watching a film, a room can use it, either one scene per phase or one chosen by a template. The scene only takes over the lights it sets. Every other light in the room keeps following the curve, and FLARE carries on adjusting it as usual. So a scene that sets just the TV backlight and one lamp leaves the rest of the room to FLARE. When the scene no longer applies, FLARE takes its lights back too, and when the room empties, FLARE still turns off the scene’s lights along with the rest of the room. On this page . | Handing a room to a scene | When the scene is applied | .

104.title: Handing a room to a scene
104.content: If you pick a Scene in one of the blueprint’s phase sections, such as Night, the room uses it during that phase. For anything a phase can’t express — a different scene while the TV is on — use Scene Template, which overrides the phase’s Scene whenever it returns one. A scene is only used if every entity it touches is in the room. A scene that reaches into another room, or doesn’t exist, is ignored and the room follows the curve.

105.title: When the scene is applied
105.content: The scene is applied when the room’s automation runs for a phase change, for motion, for an Additional Trigger, when you run it by hand, or when a light comes back online — but not on the regular update. Re-applying it every minute would undo anything you changed by hand while it was on. Like the curve, a scene never lights an empty room. If the phase changes while nobody’s there, the scene is applied when someone next walks in.

106.title: Schedules
106.content: A schedule sets when each of the four phases starts, and the brightness and colour temperature in each phase. Adding FLARE creates your schedules. You can add more, for example for rooms that need different timing, with Settings → Devices & Services → FLARE → Add schedule. On this page . | A schedule’s entities | The schedule sensor | Transitions | Copying a schedule | .

108.title: The schedule sensor
108.content: | Attribute | Description | . | state | The phase: Morning, Day, Evening or Night. | . | phase | Same as the sensor’s state. | . | brightness | The current brightness, 0–255. | . | color_temp_kelvin | The current colour temperature, in Kelvin. | . | rgb_color | The current colour temperature as [r, g, b]. | . | morning_start, day_start, evening_start, night_start | Today’s phase start times, as timestamps. | . | evening_earliest, evening_latest | Today’s earliest and latest Evening start, as timestamps. | . | points | The whole day as 289 {t, brightness, kelvin} samples, used by the chart. | . The sensor updates every minute. While the phase is overridden, every attribute except points follows the overridden phase.

109.title: Transitions
109.content: A phase’s transition is how long before the phase ends that its brightness or colour starts easing toward the next phase’s values. The change finishes when the next phase starts — for example, if Morning starts at 06:00, the lights reach Morning’s values at 06:00. Likewise, day_kelvin_transition is how many minutes before the end of Day that the colour starts easing toward Evening’s colour temperature. | A transition of 0 switches at the boundary. | A transition longer than its phase covers the whole phase. | . Brightness and colour have separate transitions. By default, Day’s colour transition is 1440 minutes, so its colour changes across the whole of Day, while its brightness changes only in roughly the last hour. Night runs past midnight, so its transition is in the minutes before Morning starts. If Night starts after midnight, Evening runs past midnight instead, and its transition is in the minutes before Night starts.

110.title: Copying a schedule
110.content: A schedule’s settings can be copied as YAML: . morning: time: "06:00" brightness: 255 kelvin: 6667 brightness_transition: 30 kelvin_transition: 30 evening: earliest: "17:00" latest: "20:00" brightness: 180 night: kelvin: 2000 . Each phase takes brightness, kelvin, brightness_transition and kelvin_transition, and a start time. Evening takes earliest and latest instead of time. When you apply a schedule, settings it leaves out keep their current values. To copy or apply a schedule, use any of: . | Copy and Paste at the bottom of each schedule on the dashboard. | Reconfigure in the schedule’s three-dot menu under FLARE → Schedules, which shows the schedule as text that you can replace and submit. | The services flare.export_schedule and flare.import_schedule. | Copy schedule and Load in the curve playground. | . A schedule with an error in it, such as an unknown setting, an invalid time or a value out of range, isn’t applied. The error message says what’s wrong.

111.title: Schedules and the curve
111.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. A schedule answers one question: what should a light look like right now? It’s a Python object (ScheduleCoordinator), the entities that hold its settings, and the entities that publish its answer.

112.title: Where a schedule’s numbers live
112.content: A schedule has no stored configuration of its own. Its settings are 21 entities, each restoring its own value across a restart: . | five time entities, the boundaries: morning_time, day_time, evening_earliest_time, evening_latest_time, night_time | sixteen number entities: each phase’s brightness and Kelvin, and how many minutes before the next phase each starts easing towards it | . They live in entity state rather than subentry.data because changing subentry data reloads the whole entry. That also makes them ordinary HA entities: an automation can change Evening’s colour with number.set_value, and the dashboard’s sliders are just these numbers. read_schedule() is the one place that reads them. It finds each entity by unique id (ScheduleInstance.current_id()), so a renamed entity is still read. It leaves out anything unreachable, and each caller decides what that means: the curve falls back to the default, and an export omits the value.

114.title: The curve maths (schedule/curve.py)
114.content: schedule/curve.py consists of pure functions, with all defaults defined in DEFAULT_CURVE_VALUES and DEFAULT_SCHEDULE_HOURS. Which phase is it? . phase_at() walks the boundaries in order: before Morning is Night, then Morning, Day, Evening, and after the Night boundary it’s Night again. A Night earlier than Morning is after midnight (_night_clock). It’s tomorrow’s boundary, and Evening runs on through midnight until it. Every timestamp is shifted onto a clock where Night comes after Evening before comparing. Tomorrow’s Morning and Night are worked out by the calendar (Boundaries.next_morning, next_night) and passed to the curve, because they aren’t 24 hours after today’s boundaries on days when daylight saving time shifts. Because flare.compute_curve takes only today’s four timestamps, it assumes 24-hour days. gantt dateFormat HH:mm axisFormat %H:%M title Night at 01:00, after midnight section Phase Evening (from yesterday) :e0, 00:00, 01:00 Night :n, 01:00, 06:00 Morning :m, 06:00, 08:00 Day :d, 08:00, 17:30 Evening :e, 17:30, 23:59 . Above, Evening runs from sunset to 01:00, and the 00:00 to 01:00 slot is still yesterday’s Evening. Without _night_clock a 01:00 Night would skip Evening altogether and start at sunset. How bright, how warm? . Each phase holds its own value, then eases linearly to the next phase’s value over its last <phase>_<brightness|kelvin>_transition minutes, so the next value arrives exactly at the boundary. The transition is clamped to the phase’s length; Day’s Kelvin default (1440 minutes) spans the whole of Day. With the default settings and a 17:30 sunset, brightness runs: . | From | To | Brightness | . | 22:00 | 05:30 | 80 (Night) | . | 05:30 | 06:00 | 80 → 255, Night’s 30-minute transition | . | 06:00 | 16:25 | 255 (Morning, then Day) | . | 16:25 | 17:30 | 255 → 180, Day’s 65-minute transition | . | 17:30 | 21:00 | 180 (Evening) | . | 21:00 | 22:00 | 180 → 80, Evening’s 60-minute transition | . day_phase is passed as an explicit parameter rather than derived from the clock, because a manual phase override supplies a phase the clock disagrees with. Every ramp clamps its interpolation factor to [0, 1] so it never extrapolates; outside that phase’s own span, an overridden phase simply returns its own target values. RGB is Kelvin converted, through HA’s color_temperature_to_rgb with a round-half-up wrapper that matches the card’s Math.round. Kept in step with JavaScript . The dashboard’s chart and the docs playground draw the same curve in JavaScript. tests/unit/dashboard/test_js_parity.py holds phase_at, phase_marks and the Night-after-midnight rule in step across the two.

115.title: The phase override
115.content: stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Auto Auto --> Overridden: select a phase<br/>(baseline = computed_phase) Overridden --> Auto: select Auto Overridden --> Auto: computed_phase moves past the baseline<br/>(unless Sticky is on) Overridden --> Overridden: refresh, same computed_phase . The select stores the computed phase at the moment it was set (the baseline). The override clears once the clock’s phase moves on, so it lasts until the next natural boundary rather than for a fixed time. switch.<slug>_sticky_phase_override turns the clearing off. The baseline isn’t saved across a restart; a restored override takes the phase at startup as its baseline.

116.title: How a room hears about it
116.content: The blueprint reads a schedule two ways: . | the Phase event entity triggers a room on a real phase change (and once after setup, so a restart repaints every room). A trigger can’t look up a device’s entities, which is why it’s an event entity on the schedule’s device and not a template. | the schedule sensor’s attributes, read in variables: for brightness, color_temp_kelvin and rgb_color. | . Between phase changes, the curve still moves within a phase, so rooms also update on their area’s tick.

117.title: Export and import
117.content: schedule/transfer.py writes a schedule as YAML keyed by phase, and reads it back. The flare.export_schedule and flare.import_schedule services use it, as do Reconfigure, the transfer card and the docs playground. | Parsed with PyYAML’s BaseLoader, so every scalar is a string. 119.title: flare.apply_lighting
119.content: Use this action to set lights to a brightness and colour temperature, turning on any that are off. It skips lights that are unavailable, already close to the target, or changed by something else (see override protection). action: flare.apply_lighting data: entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] brightness: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'brightness') }}" color_temp_kelvin: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'color_temp_kelvin') }}" transition: 2 brightness_levels: { light.kitchen_2: 60 } room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" . This sets both kitchen lights to the Home schedule’s current colour temperature, with light.kitchen_1 at the schedule’s brightness and light.kitchen_2 at 60. See brightness levels. | . | color_temp_kelvinKelvin | yes | The colour temperature. | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to set. | . | forceboolean; default false | no | Sets every light, including ones someone else has changed. For an rgb_color target, the channels’ differences added together can be up to twice this. | . | prefer_rgb_colorboolean; default false | no | Sends rgb_color instead of color_temp_kelvin to lights that support RGB. | . | rgb_color[r, g, b] or null | no | The colour for RGB lights when prefer_rgb_color is on. The schedule sensor’s rgb_color attribute provides the colour temperature converted to RGB. If rgb_color is omitted or null (or prefer_rgb_color is off), FLARE sends color_temp_kelvin instead. | . | room_entitieslist of light entity IDs | no | The room’s lights, which FLARE releases together once none of them is on. If omitted, FLARE tracks only the lights this room’s calls have set. | . | room_idtext | no | The room to record the change for, usually the calling automation: {{ this.entity_id }}. Without it, FLARE records nothing and doesn’t leave any light alone. See rooms. | . | transitionseconds, 0–300; default 0 | no | How long the change takes. Two-step bulbs spend half of it on brightness and half on colour. | . Brightness levels . | Value | Effect | . | 1–255 | Sets the light to this brightness. | . | 0 | Turns the light off. | . | null or false | Leaves the light alone, whether it’s on or off. | . 120.title: flare.turn_off
120.content: Use this action to turn lights off while keeping them controlled. It sets each light’s claim to off before turning it off, so the light still matches its claim and comes on with the rest of the room next time. action: flare.turn_off data: entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] transition: 15 . flare.turn_off or light.turn_off? . Both turn the light off, but they leave its claim saying different things: . |   | light.turn_off | flare.turn_off | . | The light’s claim | Still says what FLARE last set, such as on at 180 | Says off | . | The light’s status | overridden, once it has been off for 30 seconds, since it doesn’t match its claim | controlled, since it matches its claim | . | The next time the room’s lights are turned on | It’s left off | It’s set with the rest, so it comes on | . Either way, once none of the room’s claimed lights is on, the room deletes its claims, and every light is set the next time the room’s lights are turned on. So if you’re turning the whole room off, it makes no difference which you use. Use light.turn_off when you want a light to stay off while the rest of the room is on, such as a lamp switched off for the evening. Use flare.turn_off when a room has emptied but a nightlight stays on, so the other lights come on again when someone returns. In a room that’s still in use, a light turned off with flare.turn_off comes back on at the next update. Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to turn off. | . | transitionseconds, 0–300; default 0 | no | How long the change takes. | . Good to know . | It turns off every light it’s given, including lights someone else has changed. To turn off only the lights FLARE is still setting, call claims_check first. | A light FLARE isn’t driving is turned off directly, just like light.turn_off. | .

123.title: flare.claims_record

Call it just before you change the entities, with the values you’re about to send. action: flare.claims_record data: entities: [light.kitchen_1] room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" targets: light.kitchen_1: { brightness: 200, color_temp_kelvin: 3000 } . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights you’re about to change. | . | room_entitieslist of light entity IDs | no | The room’s lights, as for apply_lighting. | . | room_idtext | yes | The room to record the claim for, usually your automation: {{ this.entity_id }}. | . | targetsmap of entity ID to values | no | What you’re about to send each entity: brightness and either color_temp_kelvin or rgb_color. | . Good to know . | Without targets, the claim records only the call itself, which Home Assistant clears after five seconds. A bulb that takes longer than that to report back won’t match the claim by value and will become overridden. | A light running an effect that keeps changing its colour won’t match its claim. Use a scene for it instead, or hand it over with a null brightness in the blueprint. | .

124.title: flare.claims_clear
124.content: Use this action to discard claims, so FLARE sets the entities again on its next update. It’s for a light that’s overridden in a room that never goes fully dark. FLARE’s Clear button does the same for every light. action: flare.claims_clear data: entities: [light.kitchen_1] . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to clear. | . Response data . Add response_variable if you want the result: cleared lists the entities that had a claim to discard.

125.title: flare.claims_override
125.content: Use this action to mark lights as changed by someone else, so FLARE leaves them alone. You don’t usually need it. A light with a claim becomes overridden automatically once something else changes it and it stops matching its claim. It’s for lights with no claim yet, such as when your automation turns lights on in a dark room and you want FLARE to leave them as they are. Without it, they’re untracked, so the room’s next update sets them to the curve. It marks each entity whether it’s on or off. A light marked this way stays overridden until its room goes dark, its claims are cleared, or a forced flare.apply_lighting takes it back. Flares call it before turning a room off or setting it to a brightness or colour. action: flare.claims_override data: entities: [light.kitchen_1] room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | entitieslist of light entity IDs | yes | The lights to mark. | . | room_entitieslist of light entity IDs | no | The room’s lights, as for apply_lighting. | . | room_idtext | yes | The room that releases them once it’s dark, usually the automation driving them. | .

126.title: flare.compute_scene_coverage
126.content: Use this action to find out which of a set of lights a scene sets, so you can apply the scene and set the other lights yourself. action: flare.compute_scene_coverage data: scene_entity_id: scene.kitchen_night scope_entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2, light.kitchen_strip] target_entities: [light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] response_variable: coverage . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | scene_entity_idscene entity ID | yes | The scene to check. | . | scope_entitieslist of entity IDs | yes | Every entity the scene is allowed to set, usually the room’s lights and other entities on the same devices. | . | target_entitieslist of entity IDs | yes | The lights to check. | . Response data . | scene_valid: true if the scene exists and every entity it sets is in scope_entities. | covered_entities: The entities the scene sets. | uncovered_entities: The entries in target_entities that the scene doesn’t set. If scene_valid is false, this includes every entity in target_entities. | . scene_valid: true covered_entities: [light.kitchen_1] uncovered_entities: [light.kitchen_2] .

127.title: flare.resolve_target
127.content: Use this action to get the list of entities that an action on a target would reach, such as the lights in an area. action: flare.resolve_target target: area_id: kitchen response_variable: kitchen . Fields . It takes a target, as an action such as light.turn_on does: any mix of entity_id, device_id, area_id, floor_id and label_id, plus exclude targets. Response data . | entities: Every entity the target reaches, of any domain, sorted. Home Assistant decides which entities those are, in the same way as when you call an action on that target: . | An entity you name directly is always included. | An entity reached through a device, area, floor or label is left out if it’s hidden. | An entity reached through a device, area or floor, or through a label on its device or area, is also left out if it’s a configuration or diagnostic entity. If a label is on the entity itself, it’s kept. | . | . entities: [binary_sensor.kitchen_motion, light.kitchen_1, light.kitchen_2] .

128.title: flare.export_schedule
128.content: Use this action to get a schedule’s settings as YAML, in the format described under copying a schedule. action: flare.export_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" response_variable: exported . Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | schedule_device_idschedule device ID | yes | The schedule to export. | . Response data . | schedule: The schedule as YAML text, keyed by phase. | .

129.title: flare.import_schedule
129.content: Use this action to set a schedule from YAML, in the format described under copying a schedule. action: flare.import_schedule data: schedule_device_id: "{{ device_id('sensor.home_flare') }}" schedule: night: time: "23:00" . This moves the start of Night to 23:00 and leaves every other setting as it is. Fields . | Field | Required | Description | . | scheduleYAML text, or YAML written in the call | yes | The settings to apply, keyed by phase. Any setting it leaves out keeps its current value. | . | schedule_device_idschedule device ID | yes | The schedule to set. | . Good to know . | If any part of schedule has an error, such as an unknown setting, an invalid time or a value out of range, none of it is applied, and the error message says what’s wrong. | .

130.title: Two-step bulbs
130.content: Some bulbs can’t change brightness and colour temperature in one command: they jump to the new value, or ignore one of the two. FLARE sends these bulbs two commands, brightness first and then colour, each taking half the transition. It recognises them in two ways: . | By make and model, from the Two-step bulb models field under FLARE → Settings → Configure. It holds one pattern per line, matched case-insensitively against "<manufacturer> <model>", and * matches anything, so *TRADFRI bulb* and IKEA* both work. The field is pre-filled with FLARE’s default patterns. Your saved list replaces those defaults entirely, so you can remove a pattern as well as add one. If you save the field empty, FLARE uses the defaults again. | By label: give the light or its device a label created with the name no_combined_transition. FLARE matches the label’s ID, which comes from the name it was created with, so renaming another label to this won’t work. | . Once you’ve saved your own list, a later FLARE release that adds a pattern won’t change it, so you’ll need to add new bulbs yourself. Keep patterns specific, because a bulb that doesn’t need two commands transitions less smoothly when it gets them.

131.title: In your own automations
131.content: If your lights already run on automations of your own, or in Node-RED or AppDaemon, you don’t have to replace them with the blueprint to get the curve and have hand-set lights left alone: anything that can call a Home Assistant action can call these services. The blueprint is one automation built on them. Keeping a room on the curve . You need a schedule for the values. If you want FLARE to leave hand-set lights alone, pass the automation itself as the room. This keeps the kitchen on the curve: . alias: Kitchen lighting triggers: - trigger: event event_type: flare_tick event_data: area_id: kitchen conditions: - condition: template value_template: "{{ area_entities('kitchen') | select('match', '^light\\.') | select('is_state', 'on') | list | count > 0 }}" actions: - action: flare.apply_lighting data: entities: "{{ area_entities('kitchen') | select('match', '^light\\.') | select('is_state', 'on') | list }}" brightness: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'brightness') }}" color_temp_kelvin: "{{ state_attr('sensor.home_flare', 'color_temp_kelvin') }}" transition: 5 room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" room_entities: "{{ area_entities('kitchen') | select('match', '^light\\.') | list }}" . It runs on the kitchen’s tick and only passes lights that are on, since apply_lighting turns on everything it’s given. Turning the room on and off is left to you. Sending the commands yourself . If you want to send light.turn_on yourself and still have FLARE leave hand-set lights alone: . | Call flare.claims_check to find out whether someone else has changed the light. | Call flare.claims_record with the values you’re about to send, so FLARE matches them later. | Call light.turn_on yourself. | . For example, this script sets the porch light to a warm 60%, unless someone has changed it since the script last set it: . alias: Porch light warm sequence: - action: flare.claims_check data: entities: [light.porch] response_variable: check - condition: template value_template: "{{ not check.results['light.porch'].blocked }}" - action: flare.claims_record data: entities: [light.porch] room_id: "{{ this.entity_id }}" targets: light.porch: { brightness: 153, color_temp_kelvin: 2200 } - action: light.turn_on target: entity_id: light.porch data: brightness: 153 color_temp_kelvin: 2200 . targets needs the brightness and either color_temp_kelvin or rgb_color you’re sending. FLARE checks the light against it later, so a light running an effect that keeps changing its colour won’t match its claim. For that, use a scene or hand the light over with a null brightness in the blueprint instead. If your automation turns lights off while some of the room’s lights stay on, use flare.turn_off; see flare.turn_off or light.turn_off?.

132.title: Services and grouping
132.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. Everything FLARE does is a service anyone can call. The blueprint is one caller, not the only one, so each service is written as a standalone tool. The field contracts live in services.yaml and the services reference. This page is about what happens inside them.

133.title: The eleven services
133.content: | Service | Kind | Registered by | Module | . | compute_curve | pure planner | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | compute_scene_coverage | pure planner | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | apply_lighting | writes | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | turn_off | writes | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_check | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_record | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_clear | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | claims_override | claims | Settings entry | services/handlers.py | . | resolve_target | lookup | async_setup (always) | services/targets.py | . | export_schedule | schedules | async_setup (always) | services/schedules.py | . | import_schedule | schedules | async_setup (always) | services/schedules.py | . The handlers are thin adapters. They read HA state into the pure planners (grouping.py, scenes.py, curve.py, override_protection.py) and send the result. The last three need nothing of an entry, so they exist as soon as the integration loads.

134.title: apply_lighting, from call to bulb
134.content: sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Caller (room automation) participant H as apply_lighting participant G as build_groups (pure) participant L as EntityLookup participant R as ClaimRegistry participant B as light.turn_on / turn_off C->>H: entities, brightness, kelvin,<br/>levels, transition, room_id H->>H: without_flares(entities) H->>G: plan(call) G->>L: reachable? overridden? already set?<br/>two-step model or label? L->>R: record(entity) (only with a room_id) G-->>H: groups H->>H: one send per non-empty list:<br/>off, combined, combined RGB,<br/>two-step, two-step RGB H->>R: async_record(written lights, context, targets) H->>B: asyncio.gather(all sends) H-->>C: groups (optional response) . Steps 3 to 9 contain no await. The registry’s writers are callbacks, so the plan and the claims are one atomic step: no state change can arrive between deciding to write a light and recording that FLARE did.

135.title: build_groups: lights to service calls
135.content: The goal is the fewest calls that move every light that needs it, and nothing that doesn’t. flowchart TB E["entities"] --> BK["bucket by the brightness each is sent:<br/>its level, else brightness;<br/>0 is off, null/false is hands-off (dropped)"] BK --> OFFQ{"bucket brightness 0?"} OFFQ -->|"yes"| OFF["needing_off:<br/>reachable, not already off,<br/>not overridden"] OFFQ -->|"no"| RGBQ{"prefer RGB and<br/>bulb supports it?"} RGBQ -->|"yes"| RGB["target_rgb:<br/>{brightness, rgb_color}"] RGBQ -->|"no"| CT["target:<br/>{brightness, color_temp_kelvin}"] RGB --> ROUTE CT --> ROUTE ROUTE["route(lights, target)"] --> W["writable:<br/>reachable and not overridden"] W --> AS{"on, already close enough,<br/>and claimed (or no room)?"} AS -->|"yes"| ALR["already_set<br/>(not sent)"] AS -->|"no"| TSQ{"two-step model<br/>or label?"} TSQ -->|"yes"| TS["two_step / two_step_rgb"] TSQ -->|"no"| CB["combined / combined_rgb"] . One definition of closeness answers both questions: is this light still showing what FLARE set? and is this light close enough that FLARE shouldn’t send a command? By default, the tolerances are 5% of the target brightness and 5 mireds of colour temperature (configured on the Settings entry, though a service call can override them). For an rgb_color target, FLARE sums the differences across the red, green, and blue channels and allows up to twice the colour tolerance (10 by default). Fixed floors handle device rounding at low values: at least 2 brightness points for dim targets, any two Kelvin values that floor to the same mired, and a summed difference of at least 4 for RGB. Because 5% brightness and 5 mireds are roughly one just-noticeable difference, any light close enough to skip sending is also never marked as changed by someone else. Both go through tracking/matching.shows(), the one place a light’s reported values are compared with a target (see Claims and override protection). Brightness is clamped to 255 (MAX_BRIGHTNESS) before it’s compared. light.turn_on silently clamps, so an unclamped target would never read as reached, and FLARE would resend it every tick. Two-step bulbs . Some bulbs (IKEA TRADFRI) drop the colour if brightness and colour change in one transition. A light goes two-step if its device’s "<manufacturer> <model>" matches a glob in the Settings entry’s Two-step bulb models, or it carries the no_combined_transition label. sequenceDiagram participant H as apply_lighting participant B as Bulb Note over H: contexts made up front:<br/>brightness ctx (secondary),<br/>colour ctx (primary) H->>B: turn_on(brightness, transition: T/2)<br/>context: brightness ctx Note over H: asyncio.sleep(T/2) H->>B: turn_on(brightness + colour, transition: T/2)<br/>context: colour ctx . Both context ids go into the claim, and a report under either counts as FLARE’s. The sleep is why claims are recorded first: a mode: restart can cancel the run mid-sleep.

136.title: turn_off
136.content: flare.turn_off records {"state": "off"} as the target on each light that already holds a claim (ClaimRegistry.async_record_off), then calls light.turn_off in a single operation without checking override protection (an empty room turns off hand-set lights too). Recording the off target is what distinguishes a FLARE turn-off from someone else switching a light off after the 5-second context expires, which matters whenever other lights keep the room from going dark (once a room is completely dark, it releases its claims anyway). turn_off takes no room_id because claimed lights already belong to their rooms, and it creates no new claims on lights that weren’t already tracked. Callers must not split this into separate claim-recording and light.turn_off calls.

137.title: Unclaimed lights
137.content: If a light is already on and showing the values apply_lighting would send, FLARE skips sending a command when the light already has a claim or when the call has no room_id. However, an unclaimed light in a tracked room is written to anyway (EntityLookup.unclaimed), so that write establishes FLARE’s claim and adds the light to the room. After pressing Clear in a lit room, this guarantees every light gets re-claimed with what FLARE actually sent rather than trusting a stale state report from a bulb that just reconnected. The trade-off is one initial write per light whenever a room starts tracking it.

138.title: resolve_target
138.content: flare.resolve_target returns the entities a target reaches by HA’s own rule (helpers/target.py, async_extract_referenced_entity_ids, with expand_group=False). It’s the same rule light.turn_on area_id: uses and a flare’s membership uses. Templates can’t apply it: they can see is_hidden_entity, but not entity_category, and device_entities() misses child devices. target_entities() in the same module is what area setup calls to decide which areas have lights.

139.title: Scene coverage
139.content: compute_scene_coverage works out which of the room’s lights a scene covers (scenes.py, generic, nothing lighting-specific). A scene counts as active only if it exists and everything it covers is within scope (the room’s entities plus every entity on each light’s device). The blueprint then sends the curve to the lights the scene doesn’t cover, and releases the claims on the ones it does.

140.title: Setup and upgrades
140.content: Part of Architecture, for contributors and the curious. Nothing here is needed to use FLARE. How FLARE gets from “Add Integration” to rooms that light themselves, and how it keeps an installed blueprint current.

141.title: The main flow
141.content: FlareConfigFlow (config_flow.py) powers the integration page’s main button. On first install it creates the entries and schedules and offers room setup; on subsequent runs it acts as Set up area. flowchart TB U(["Add Integration / Set up area"]) --> Q{"Schedules entry exists?"} Q -->|"no: first setup"| S["schedules:<br/>Home, one per floor, or Custom"] S -->|"Custom, or floor names<br/>that fail the checks"| SN["schedule_names"] S --> CE SN --> CE["_create_entries():<br/>Schedules, Settings, Flares<br/>via SOURCE_IMPORT"] CE --> AU{"automations menu<br/>(skipped with no lit areas)"} AU -->|"Skip for now"| SUM AU -->|"set up areas"| AR Q -->|"yes"| AR["areas:<br/>a schedule dropdown per area,<br/>grouped by floor"] AR --> AS["area_setup.async_set_up_areas():<br/>an automation per area"] AS --> FM{"flares menu"} FM -->|"Skip"| SUM FM -->|"pick rooms"| FR["flare_rooms:<br/>room flares, all ticked"] FR --> SUM(["abort: setup_complete / areas_set_up,<br/>with a summary"]) . | The entries are created through SOURCE_IMPORT: the flow starts a hidden import flow for each missing one. Each entry type has a fixed unique id (flare_schedules, flare_tracking, flare_flares), so there’s only ever one of each, and deleting one and adding it back works. | The flow ends on an abort carrying a summary, never on an entry. HA’s “integration added” dialog would put every device of the entry the flow completes on through a rename-and-place form, with no way to suppress it. | First setup raises a repair linking to a page reload, since a page open during setup never loads the dashboard’s JavaScript (see Dashboard internals). | .

142.title: Subentry and options flows
142.content: | Flow | Where | Does | . | SensorSubentryFlow | Schedules entry, Add schedule | a new schedule; Reconfigure shows it as YAML to copy out or replace, and applying sets the entities, leaving the subentry untouched | . | FlareSubentryFlow | Flares entry, Add flare | a flare over a FLARE-blueprint automation, or a custom one by input | . | FlareOptionsFlow | Settings entry, Configure | update interval, gap between areas, matching tolerances, and two-step bulb models | . Reconfiguring a subentry ends with async_update_and_abort. Subentry changes don’t reload an entry by themselves, so each entry has an update listener (_async_reload_entry) that does. It yields once (asyncio.sleep(0)), so several subentries added in one go, as area setup does, reload the entry once.

143.title: Area setup (area_setup.py)
143.content: sequenceDiagram participant F as config flow participant A as area_setup participant Y as automations.yaml participant HA as automation integration F->>A: async_set_up_areas({area: schedule}) A->>A: one config per area:<br/>use_blueprint flare/flare.yaml,<br/>schedule device, room_target {area_id} A->>HA: async_validate_config_item (each) A->>Y: read, append, write_utf8_file_atomic A->>HA: automation.reload alt the entities appear A->>A: put each automation in its area,<br/>label it FLARE else they don't (configuration.yaml<br/>doesn't include the file) A->>Y: restore the original text, byte for byte end . It writes automations.yaml the way HA’s own automation editor does (components/config/automation.py), because there’s no public API for it. A lock in hass.data keeps two setups from interleaving. | Which areas are offered: every area holding a light by HA’s own rule (target_entities({"area_id": ...})), so an area with only hidden or categorised lights isn’t offered. | “Already set up” means an automation labelled FLARE sits in the area. That leaves the area’s schedule dropdown empty by default; picking a schedule for it and submitting creates another automation. | Not handled yet: a failure part-way leaves what was already created. | .

144.title: Keeping the blueprint current
144.content: HA never installs a custom integration’s blueprints, so FLARE checks for its own once HA has started (async_at_started), from the Settings entry. flowchart TB start(["HA started"]) --> ours{"any blueprint<br/>named FLARE?"} ours -->|"no"| miss["repair: blueprint_not_installed<br/>Fix installs flare/flare.yaml"] ours -->|"yes"| used{"used by an automation,<br/>and stamped older than<br/>this release, or in<br/>another language?"} used -->|"yes"| old["repair: outdated_blueprint<br/>Fix writes the shipped file<br/>over each stale copy"] used -->|"no"| ok(["clear both repairs"]) . | Ours is recognised by name, “FLARE”. Only copies an automation uses count as outdated: HA never removes an unused copy, and a repair about an unused blueprint couldn’t be silenced. | The version stamp is in the blueprint’s description, since the blueprint: block is a closed schema and the description survives every import route. It’s 0.0.0-dev in source. scripts/release.py writes the real version into each release’s zip, along with the manifest and BLUEPRINT_VERSION. | The blueprint is written in HA’s language (blueprint_translation.py). Home Assistant doesn’t natively translate blueprints, so _shipped() substitutes each input’s text from blueprints/translations/<language>.yaml before saving the file. Keys, defaults, and selectors stay unchanged, and select options keep their English values behind translated labels. The version stamp includes the language (Blueprint version 2.0.0 (de)), so a copy whose language differs from Home Assistant’s counts as outdated and Fix rewrites it. A stamp without a language suffix is treated as English. | A blueprint that fails to load comes back from async_get_blueprints() as the exception itself, hence isinstance rather than a None check. | .

145.title: Migrations
145.content: async_migrate_entry handles version 3. Minor version 1 to 2 is FLARE 2.0: it removes the old zone subentries (taking their devices, entities and claims with them) and retitles a “Zones” entry “Settings”. Dropping the claims fails open, since FLARE takes every room back on its next update.

146.title: Getting a build onto a real house
146.content: HACS installs only released zips, so a development build is written over an installed release file by file. The steps are in CLAUDE.md (“Getting a build onto the live instance”). Try it in the sandbox first.

147.title: Templates
147.content: The blueprint’s settings work per phase and for the whole room, so on their own they can’t dim the lights while the TV is on, keep one lamp as the nightlight, or leave a light to another automation. The three template inputs, in the blueprint’s Custom section, cover cases like these, because each one is a Home Assistant template that can depend on anything and set each light separately. The Blueprint page lists what each one accepts. On this page . | Brightness Template . | Dimming a light while the TV is on | Dimming some lights in the evening | Leaving a light alone | One level for the whole room | A level that follows the curve | A light that never drops below a level | 0 or null? | . | Idle Brightness Template . | One lamp as the nightlight | A whole-room nightlight | A nightlight that follows the sun | . | Scene Template | .

148.title: Brightness Template
148.content: Returns the brightness each light should sit at, as a mapping from entity ID to a level: . | Value | Effect | . | 1–255 | The light sits at this brightness, on the same scale as the phase brightnesses | . | '50%' | The light sits at this percentage of full brightness: '100%' is 255, '50%' is 128 | . | 'x0.5' | The light sits at the curve’s brightness multiplied by this, so it still follows the curve | . | 0 | The light is turned off | . | null or false | FLARE leaves the light alone entirely, on or off | . A light the template doesn’t mention follows the curve as usual, so return {} when the template has nothing to change. Dimming a light while the TV is on . {{ {'light.lounge_ceiling': 40} if is_state('media_player.tv', 'playing') else {} }} . While the TV plays, the ceiling light sits at 40 and the rest of the room follows the curve. Add a State trigger on media_player.tv to Additional Triggers so the room changes as soon as the TV starts or stops, rather than at the next update. Dimming some lights in the evening . {% set phase = states('sensor.home_flare') %} {% if phase == 'Evening' %} {{ {'light.kitchen_1': 20, 'light.kitchen_2': 20} }} {% elif phase == 'Night' %} {{ {'light.kitchen_1': 5, 'light.kitchen_2': 5} }} {% else %} {{ {} }} {% endif %} . The rest of the kitchen follows the curve; these two sit lower once Evening starts. Leaving a light alone . {{ {'light.kitchen_strip': none} if states('sensor.home_flare') in ['Evening', 'Night'] else {} }} . In the evening another automation runs a gradient on the kitchen strip, so this hands the strip over during Evening and Night and FLARE leaves it alone. FLARE won’t turn it off when the room empties either; the other automation needs to do that. One level for the whole room . A single value applies to every light in the room: . {{ '15%' if is_state('media_player.tv', 'playing') else none }} . none here means “no opinion”, so the room follows the curve when the TV is off. A level that follows the curve . A number or a percentage is fixed: the light stays at it for as long as the template returns it, whatever the time of day. To keep a light at, say, half the room’s brightness, multiply the curve instead: . {{ {'light.lounge_ceiling': 'x0.5'} }} . 'x1.5' makes a light brighter than the rest of the room, up to full brightness. A light that never drops below a level . brightness is the brightness, 0–255, the room’s schedule is at right now, which is what every light without a level gets. Use it for anything a multiplier can’t do, such as a floor: . {{ {'light.desk_lamp': [brightness, 80] | max} }} . The desk lamp follows the curve, but never sits below 80. brightness is none while the schedule is unavailable, so a template doing arithmetic with it can guard with brightness is not none. 0 or null? . 0 turns the light off but keeps it FLARE’s, so it comes back on with the rest of the room. null hands the light over completely: FLARE doesn’t touch it at all, so it isn’t turned off when the room empties either, and whatever controls it has to do that instead. When the template returns a light, its value overrides the phase’s Lights Off for that light.

149.title: Idle Brightness Template
149.content: Returns what each light dims to when the room is empty instead of going dark (1–255, or a percentage like '5%'). It accepts the same values as Brightness Template except 'x0.5', since an empty room has no curve brightness to multiply. When it returns a light, its value overrides the phase’s Idle Brightness for that light. Returning 0, '0%', null, or false turns that light off when the room empties — unlike Brightness Template, null here does not leave the light alone while the room is empty. Return {} when you have nothing to override for a light. One lamp as the nightlight . {{ {'light.landing_lamp': 20} }} . With the phase settings at 0, this lamp stays at 20 when the landing empties and every other light goes out. When a phase’s setting is 0, only the lights the template names have an idle brightness in that phase. So a template naming one lamp makes that lamp the room’s only nightlight, even if you only meant to give it a different level from the rest. To keep the rest dim too, set the phase’s Idle Brightness as well, and use the template for the one light. A whole-room nightlight . A single value applies to every light in the room: . {{ 20 }} . A nightlight that follows the sun . The Night phase starts at a fixed time, not at dark. For a hall that stays dimly lit whenever it’s dark outside, leave the four phase settings at 0 and use the sun: . {{ 10 if is_state('sun.sun', 'below_horizon') else {} }} . {} means “no opinion”, so the hall goes fully dark while the sun is up. The hall picks up the change at the next update after sunset, which can be up to a minute later. Don’t add a trigger on sun.sun to Additional Triggers to make it immediate: at sunrise that would bring the lights up to the curve instead of turning them off.

150.title: Scene Template
150.content: Returns a scene’s entity ID, to hand the room to that scene instead of the curve. It overrides the phase’s Scene whenever it returns a scene that exists. {{ 'scene.lounge_movie' if is_state('media_player.tv', 'playing') else '' }} . Return '' for no scene. See Scene handoff for how a room shares itself with a scene.
